reviewer_checklist.title: Credible understanding of practice
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the materials give students a credible understanding of how this topic shows up in professional practice. Indicate where the material feels realistic, artificial, outdated, oversimplified or incomplete.

reviewer_checklist.title: Current relevance in the field
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the materials reflect the way this topic is currently discussed, used or implemented in the field. Suggest additions or updates where important tools, methods, standards, regulations, debates or developments are missing.

reviewer_checklist.title: Relevance for the track and job roles
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the materials are relevant for the track and for at least one of the intended job roles. Indicate where the link to professional roles, responsibilities, tasks or decisions could be made clearer.

reviewer_checklist.title: Professional judgement
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the material helps students develop professional judgement, rather than only learn definitions, concepts or procedures. Indicate where students could be asked to make, justify or evaluate decisions.

reviewer_checklist.title: Use of concepts, methods or tools
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the material helps students understand not only what a concept, method or tool is, but also when, why and how it should be used in practice. Indicate where practical use cases, conditions for use or limitations could be made clearer.

reviewer_checklist.title: Risks, trade-offs and implementation challenges
reviewer_checklist.detail: Assess whether the material addresses relevant risks, limitations, trade-offs, uncertainty, implementation barriers or ethical issues. Suggest additions where students need a more realistic understanding of what can go wrong or what makes implementation difficult.

review_process.rule: Put reviews in the wiki Discussion section of the related LE
review_process.detail: Not by email — so the review is documented in the right place.

review_process.rule: Propose a minor or major revision of the learning material
review_process.detail: Every review should state whether minor or major revision is needed.

review_process.rule: Sign your review with your name (and ideally email)
review_process.detail: Reviewers may involve colleagues; signing lets authors trace who reviewed and contact them for clarification.

review_process.rule: The slides (learning materials) are the PRIMARY review target
review_process.detail: Lesson plans need lighter review — they're re-evaluated together with the slides. Review the materials first, then re-check the plan against them.

guides.review_process_note: Post reviews in the wiki Discussion section of the LE (never email), with a minor/major revision suggestion, signed with your name — so authors can trace and contact the reviewer.
guides.reviewer_role_summary: RealAI reviews as the 'Reviewer' role: judge whether materials are credible, current and relevant from a specialist & professional-practice perspective. The slides are the primary target; the lesson plan is re-evaluated together with them.

sharepoint.note: Learning materials (slides) upload to the Utrecht SharePoint WP4 folder; the PPT template is in its Templates subfolder. No access? Ask the track lead.

claude_howto.how: Open the LE page in Chrome and ask Claude to draft Learning Outcomes, a detailed teacher guide, or literature for 'Expected preparation'. It reads the page directly; keep edits on the wiki.

Upload slides to the Utrecht SharePoint WP4 folder (PPT template in Templates). Use Claude in the deck to draft content + use PPT speaker-notes (remarks) for teach-info you don't want on the slide itself. Make slides self-explanatory — different teachers will deliver them.

wiki_sections.text:
BSAIC-09
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the claim that strategy lives and dies in the operating model. An AI strategy the operating model cannot execute is a document, not a strategy, and the session exists to make the execution discipline visible and teachable.
Introduce the AI operating model archetypes. Define a centralised Centre of Excellence as the pattern in which AI capability is concentrated for leverage and consistency, a federated model as the pattern in which business units own their own AI capability for pace and relevance, and a hybrid model as the attempt to combine the two through a shared platform and distributed delivery. Walk through the decision logic that points to each archetype and show named examples from the banking, retail, and industrial sectors.
Move to RACI matrix design. Show how decision rights in AI systems span data stewards, model owners, business sponsors, and risk functions, and how a poorly designed RACI produces the characteristic AI failure mode of an incident with no accountable owner. Work through a RACI for an AI model that makes a materially impactful decision, and make the accountabilities concrete.
Cover process redesign for AI integration. Identify the human decision nodes that AI can inform, augment, or replace, and show how the redesign is not a one-to-one substitution but a rethinking of the process itself. Use a credit-decisioning or demand-forecasting example to make the redesign visible.
Address cross-functional teaming. Define the composition and charter of an effective AI product team: the technical lead, the domain expert, the risk representative, the product owner, and the business sponsor. Show how charter confusion produces team dysfunction and how explicit decision rights prevent it.
Close the content with change management. Role displacement, capability gaps, and resistance to new accountability structures are the predictable human responses to operating model redesign. Name the specific interventions, coaching, communication, and capability development, that the literature shows to be effective, and connect them to the work done in the Leadership workstream.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to architect a target operating model that specifies decision rights and the interface between centralised and federated functions, trace the dependencies between use cases, processes, and roles to identify where current choices will constrain scaling, and make a reasoned case for a CoE, federated, or hybrid pattern with explicit trade-offs in accountability and pace.
"

wiki_sections.text:
BSAIC-10
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the observation that most enterprise AI portfolios resemble a shopping list more than a strategy. The shopping-list portfolio has a technical name, a portfolio of point solutions without foundational investments, and the failure mode it produces is well documented and expensive.
Introduce AI project interdependencies and foundational-capability sequencing. Investments in data platforms, MLOps infrastructure, identity and access management, and model governance enable and gate downstream use cases. Show a concrete example where three downstream use cases all depended on the same absent foundational investment, and the portfolio delivered only one of them because the others were starved of the prerequisite. Introduce the sequencing discipline of quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, arranged so that each phase unlocks the next.
Move to risk-adjusted portfolio scoring. Walk through a multi-criteria prioritisation matrix that incorporates technical debt, regulatory exposure, talent availability, data readiness, and strategic alignment. Show the weighting trade-offs that differ by industry and by the organisation's position on its maturity curve, and connect this to the maturity model work in BSAIC-16. Make explicit the difference between scoring for comparison and scoring for decision, and why the scoring instrument itself needs to be calibrated before it is trusted.
Address the staged investment logic. Quick wins build credibility and release resources, capability builders remove the foundational constraints that gate the rest of the portfolio, and flagship transformations deliver the strategic intent. Show how mis-sequencing produces programme failure even when each individual project is well managed.
Explore the communication discipline. Translating a technical sequencing logic into a Board-ready investment narrative is a specialist act. Walk through the narrative structure: the strategic frame, the dependency map, the staged investment ask, and the forward-looking risk posture. Contrast this with the project-by-project approval pattern that produces portfolio incoherence.
Close the content with the failure modes. Approving point solutions without their prerequisites, neglecting dependencies, under-investing in foundational capabilities, and substituting a list of initiatives for a coherent roadmap. Name each and the specific preventive discipline.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to curate a risk-adjusted portfolio that sequences quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, rank-order initiatives against a defensible multi-criteria instrument, trace foundational dependencies and diagnose the point-solution failure mode, and communicate the roadmap to a simulated Board as an investment narrative that survives cross-examination.
"

wiki_sections.text:
BSAIC-11
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open by naming the central design choice. Every AI deployment makes a decision about where humans and machines sit on the work, and most organisations make that decision implicitly, by default, rather than by design. The session exists to make it a deliberate act.
Introduce the augmentation-automation spectrum. Define augmentation as AI supporting a human whose judgement remains primary, and automation as AI executing without routine human involvement. Anchor the discussion in the theoretical foundations from Brynjolfsson and McAfee, and show how current enterprise practice has evolved the spectrum into a more granular set of design patterns.
Move to task decomposition methodology. Show how a role breaks down into tasks, and each task into subtasks, and how each subtask can be assessed for where value sits on the human-machine boundary. Use a knowledge-work role, legal document review, radiology, or financial analysis, and walk through the decomposition in detail. Make the exercise concrete, not theoretical.
Introduce cognitive load theory as the design constraint that most human-AI systems ignore. Working memory is finite, and poorly designed AI interfaces overwhelm practitioners with alerts, recommendations, and probabilistic scores that cannot be usefully integrated. Show how interfaces that respect cognitive load, by summarising rather than streaming and by prioritising rather than enumerating, produce measurably better outcomes.
Work through organisational case studies. Radiological diagnosis, where AI augments the radiologist's reading, legal document review, where AI pre-filters and classifies, and financial analysis, where AI triangulates signals across noisy sources. Make clear what worked, what did not, and what the design choices were that differentiated the outcomes.
Close the content with measurement. Productivity metrics alone are insufficient because they miss decision quality and practitioner wellbeing. Walk through the full measurement stack and show why a single-metric view produces gaming and burnout, both of which defeat the deployment's original purpose.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to deconstruct a knowledge-work role into its constituent tasks and map each against the augmentation-automation spectrum with reference to complementarity and cognitive-load evidence, design a human-AI dyad that specifies task division, support form, and oversight interface, and contest the implicit assumptions behind a proposed automation design about where value and risk sit on the human-machine boundary.
"

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
"Start by grounding the session in the ordinary finance-and-control task of explaining what changed, why it changed, and what requires attention. Briefly show how variance analysis and management commentary are traditionally produced, then introduce AI as a support layer that can draft explanations, highlight unusual movements, and help prioritize what finance teams should look at first.
Use a case with budget, actual, and prior-period figures, plus a small set of AI-generated commentary snippets and anomaly flags. Ask students to judge which comments are genuinely useful, which are too generic, which anomalies are material enough to escalate, and where human interpretation is still needed to connect numbers to business reality. The key teaching point is that AI can accelerate reporting work, but that decision-useful commentary depends on context, materiality, and professional judgment rather than fluent text alone."

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
"Start by anchoring the session in the basic purpose of credit modelling: estimating risk in order to support lending and portfolio decisions. Introduce a progression from more interpretable approaches, such as scorecards or logistic regression, to more complex machine-learning models, and make clear that the central issue is not technical sophistication for its own sake, but what is gained and what is lost as models become harder to interpret.
Then use a case in which students compare two stylized models for the same credit decision problem: one simpler and easier to explain, the other more complex and potentially more accurate. Ask them to discuss not only which model appears stronger statistically, but what each model allows a bank, lender, borrower, or supervisor to understand and challenge. The key teaching point is that in credit modelling, model choice is not only a performance question but also a governance and decision-rights question."

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should introduce adversarial attacks as a reliability and safety problem in machine learning, not as a practical hacking tutorial. The goal is that students understand why ML systems may fail under deliberate manipulation, what kinds of failures are possible, and how this changes evaluation and deployment thinking.
Use intuitive examples throughout, such as a slightly modified image that fools a classifier, a spam email rewritten to bypass detection, fraudulent transactions shaped to look normal, poisoned training examples, or a user prompt designed to make an AI assistant ignore instructions. Keep examples conceptual and avoid step-by-step attack recipes.
The central intuition should be: a model can perform well on ordinary test data and still be fragile when inputs are chosen by an adaptive adversary. Standard accuracy is therefore not enough when a system is deployed in an environment where someone has an incentive to make it fail.
A good lecture arc is:
• what adversarial attacks are and why they matter,
   • how adversarial examples differ from ordinary errors,
   • what broad attack surfaces exist in the ML lifecycle,
   • why modern ML models can be vulnerable,
   • how adversarial risk should influence validation, monitoring, and deployment.
Keep the mathematical and algorithmic details light. It is acceptable to mention perturbations, decision boundaries, gradients, and high-dimensional spaces at an intuitive level, but do not teach attack algorithms in detail. The lecture should stay appropriate for a mixed-background horizontal audience.
Make the difference between accidental distribution shift and adversarial manipulation explicit. Both can cause failures, but adversarial settings are harder because the data-generating process reacts to the deployed system.
End with a balanced message. Adversarial robustness cannot usually be guaranteed absolutely, but threat modelling, appropriate testing, monitoring, secure data pipelines, and human oversight can reduce risk substantially.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce adversarial attacks using simple scenarios: a manipulated image classifier, a spam filter bypass, fraud detection, or a malicious prompt to an AI assistant.
   • Define an adversarial attack as an intentional attempt to make a machine learning system produce an incorrect, unsafe, or unintended output.
   • Contrast adversarial failures with ordinary model errors and random noise.
10 - 20 minutes
• Explain why standard test performance may be misleading when future inputs are chosen by an adaptive adversary.
   • Introduce the idea of a threat model: who can attack, what they can observe, what they can change, and what they want to achieve.
   • Discuss common goals of attackers: misclassification, bypassing detection, causing denial of service, extracting information, or manipulating downstream decisions.
20 - 30 minutes
• Present the main attack surfaces across the ML lifecycle: training data, feature pipeline, model interface, input data at inference time, outputs, and feedback loops.
   • Differentiate high-level attack types: evasion at inference time, data poisoning during training, model extraction, membership or privacy inference, and prompt or input manipulation in AI systems.
   • Use examples to show that attacks are not limited to images; they can affect text, tabular data, signals, recommender systems, and operational workflows.
30 - 40 minutes
• Explain intuitively why adversarial vulnerability can occur: high-dimensional inputs, brittle decision boundaries, shortcut learning, overconfidence, spurious correlations, and mismatch between training and deployment.
   • Discuss how small changes can be irrelevant to a human but important to a model, or alternatively realistic changes can exploit known model shortcuts.
   • Connect adversarial vulnerability to the broader themes of robustness, validation, and uncertainty.
40 - 50 minutes
• Discuss consequences

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should give students a compact statistical intuition for why numerical results and model predictions are never exact. It should not become a mathematical statistics course. The emphasis is on interpretation, communication, and decision-making under uncertainty.
Use one running example throughout, such as a medical risk prediction model, a loan default model, or a quality-control classifier. Revisit the same example when explaining estimates, confidence intervals, predicted probabilities, calibration, and threshold-based decisions.
The key intuition should be: statistical results are summaries of imperfect evidence. Good statistical reasoning asks not only “what is the number?”, but also “how uncertain is it?”, “what population does it apply to?”, and “can the predicted probabilities be trusted?”
A useful lecture arc is:
• why uncertainty appears even in clean-looking datasets,
   • how samples lead to estimates rather than exact truths,
   • how uncertainty can be quantified and visualized,
   • why probabilistic predictions need calibration,
   • and why calibrated probabilities matter for responsible decisions.
Keep formulas minimal. A simple mean/proportion, a confidence interval, and a reliability diagram are enough. Avoid deep derivations of probability theory, Bayesian inference, asymptotic theory, or advanced scoring rules.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce uncertainty through a familiar decision problem: e.g. a model says a patient has 20% risk, or a study reports that treatment A is better than treatment B.
   • Ask what would make the number trustworthy or misleading.
   • Define the lecture scope: uncertainty in data, estimates, predictions, and decisions.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explain sources of uncertainty: sampling variability, measurement error, missing data, label noise, population heterogeneity, and model assumptions.
   • Distinguish variability in the world from uncertainty in our knowledge about the world.
   • Use small examples to show why two samples from the same population can give different results.
25 - 40 minutes
• Introduce estimates, standard error, confidence intervals, and the idea that a result is a range of plausible values rather than a single exact value.
   • Clarify common misinterpretations: a confidence interval is not a guarantee for one individual, and statistical significance is not the same as practical importance.
   • Briefly compare uncertainty for a mean/proportion with uncertainty for a model performance metric.
40 - 55 minutes
• Explain prediction uncertainty: why a model output may be uncertain even if the fitted model is fixed.
   • Distinguish confidence intervals around an average effect from prediction intervals or predicted probabilities for individual cases.
   • Connect uncertainty to classification thresholds and the cost of false positives and false negatives.
55 - 70 minutes
• Introduce probabilistic predictions and calibration: among cases predicted as 20% risk, roughly 20% should experience the event.
   • Distinguish calibration from discrimination: a model can rank cases well but still produce overconfident or underconfident probabilities.
   • Introduce reliability diagrams/calibration curves, Brier score, and log loss at an intuitive level.
70 - 82 minutes
• Discuss miscalibration under dataset shift, subgroup differences, small samples, and overfitting.
   • Explain why recalibration may be necessary before deployment in a new population.
   • Use the running example to show how the same AUROC can support very different decisions depending on calibration.
82 - 90 minutes
• Summarize the practical checklist: What is the target population? How uncertain is the estimate? Are the probabilities calibrated? What decision threshold is used? What happens if the estimate is wrong?
   • Final takeaway: statistics is not a way to remove uncertainty; it is a way to make uncertainty visible, interpretable, and usable.

This lecture should present robustness and validation as the “reality check” part of statistics and machine learning. The central question is not whether a result can be obtained, but whether it survives when we change the sample, assumptions, preprocessing, validation split, metric, or deployment context.
Use one running example throughout, ideally the same type of example used in H_128: a medical risk prediction model, a credit-risk model, or a quality-control model. Show how the model may look good during development but fail when evaluated on genuinely new data or a different subgroup.
The key intuition should be: a result is more credible when it is stable under reasonable perturbations and tested against data that were not used, directly or indirectly, to build it.
A useful lecture arc is:
• generalization as the goal of validation,
   • why train/test separation is necessary but not sufficient,
   • how leakage and repeated information create false confidence,
   • how external and subgroup validation reveal fragility,
   • and how robustness checks complement formal metrics.
Keep the lecture practical. Students should leave with a validation checklist they can apply to AI papers, projects, and deployed systems. Avoid spending too much time on the mathematics of resampling; focus on what each validation design can and cannot prove.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce a failure scenario: a model performs very well in development but fails in another hospital, another year, another device, or another user group.
   • Define validation and robustness in plain language.
   • Connect back to H_128: uncertainty tells us how precise evidence appears; validation asks whether the evidence travels.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explain generalization and the difference between training performance and performance on genuinely new cases.
   • Introduce overfitting as learning patterns that do not repeat.
   • Distinguish model development, model selection, and final evaluation.
25 - 40 minutes
• Explain train-validation-test splits, cross-validation, and why the final test set should be touched only once.
   • Discuss when random splits are reasonable and when grouped, temporal, patient-level, site-level, or geographical splits are needed.
   • Emphasize that the split must match the intended future use of the system.
40 - 55 minutes
• Discuss common validation failures: leakage, duplicated patients, preprocessing before splitting, target leakage, hyperparameter tuning on the test set, and labels that encode future information.
   • Use examples where leakage produces impressive but meaningless performance.
   • Give students a practical leakage-detection checklist.
55 - 68 minutes
• Explain metric choice and metric uncertainty: AUROC, accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, calibration metrics, and confidence intervals around performance.
   • Connect metrics to decision context: class imbalance, asymmetric costs, and threshold-dependent behavior.
   • Stress that no single metric validates a system.
68 - 80 minutes
• Introduce external validation, temporal validation, and subgroup validation.
   • Discuss distribution shift and why a model can fail without any coding error.
   • Use the running example to show how performance can differ across sites, devices, demographic groups, or time periods.
80 - 90 minutes
• Introduce robustness checks: sensitivity analyses, alternative preprocessing choices, baseline comparisons, ablations, negative controls, perturbation tests, and stress tests.
   • Summarize a validation report structure: data split, leakage prevention, metrics with uncertainty, subgroup/external validation, robustness checks, and known limitations.
   • Final takeaway: validation is not a ceremonial test at the end; it is the design logic that tells us whether a result deserves trust.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This practical should convert the ideas from H_128 and H_129 into a small but complete statistical workflow. Students should work with a prepared dataset and a prepared notebook or spreadsheet template, so the session is about reasoning rather than debugging.
Use a simple binary prediction task with predicted probabilities. Suitable examples include a synthetic medical risk dataset, loan default, equipment failure, readmission risk, or quality-control defect prediction. The dataset should include at least one grouping variable, such as site, year, device, hospital, user group, or demographic subgroup, so that validation and robustness can be demonstrated.
A Python notebook with pre-written helper functions is recommended: students should edit only a few lines, interpret plots, and fill in short conclusions.
The key intuition should be: statistical practice is an iterative chain of questions. What is the estimate? How uncertain is it? Are the predicted probabilities calibrated? Does the result survive a different split or subgroup? What would we report honestly?
The teacher should avoid turning the session into a programming exercise. Provide working code for data loading, plotting, and model fitting. The main student activity should be interpretation, comparison, and critical evaluation.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce the dataset, prediction target, variables, and intended decision context.
   • Clarify the output expected from students: a short statistical report or worksheet with plots, metrics, and conclusions.
   • Remind students of the H_128/H_129 checklist: uncertainty, calibration, validation, robustness.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explore the data: sample size, outcome prevalence, missingness, subgroup/site/year composition, and basic descriptive statistics.
   • Ask students to identify what the unit of analysis is and what future population the result should apply to.
   • Discuss whether a random split would be appropriate or whether grouped/temporal validation would be more realistic.
25 - 45 minutes
• Compute simple uncertainty summaries: confidence interval or bootstrap interval for outcome prevalence and one performance metric.
   • Compare a point estimate with its interval and discuss what the interval changes in the interpretation.
   • Ask students to write one cautious sentence that reports the estimate with uncertainty.
45 - 65 minutes
• Fit or load a simple probabilistic model, such as logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, or gradient boosting model.
   • Evaluate discrimination using AUROC or a similar ranking metric.
   • Compare training and test performance and identify signs of overfitting or overly optimistic evaluation.
65 - 82 minutes
• Construct a calibration curve or reliability table from predicted probabilities.
   • Compute or inspect Brier score/log loss and compare this with AUROC.
   • Discuss cases where the model ranks well but gives poorly calibrated probabilities.
82 - 98 minutes
• Explore threshold-based decisions: choose one threshold and compute sensitivity, specificity, false positives, and false negatives.
   • Discuss how the “best” threshold depends on the cost of mistakes and the use context.
   • Ask students whether the same threshold would be acceptable for all subgroups.
98 - 112 minutes
• Run at least two robustness checks: alternative random seed/split, subgroup evaluation, temporal/site holdout, missing-data perturbation, or comparison with a simple baseline.
   • Record which conclusions are stable and which change.
   • Discuss whether observed instability is random noise, real heterogeneity, or a validation-design problem.
112 - 120 minutes
• Students write a short conclusion: main result, uncertainty, calibration, validation design, robustness findings, and limitations.
   • Brief group discussion: what would be needed before using the model in practice?
   • Final takeaway: practical statistics is not the production of one met

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This interactive session should teach students how an AI project is normally structured in practice. It should not be a deep technical lesson about algorithms, nor a generic project-management lecture. The focus is the bridge between an AI idea and a working, validated, maintainable system.
Use one running case throughout the session, preferably a realistic but simple project such as medical risk prediction, customer-support email triage, predictive maintenance, document classification, or demand forecasting. The same case should be revisited from multiple angles: stakeholders, data, labels, baseline, model, validation, deployment, monitoring, and risks.
The central intuition should be: a successful AI project is not mainly about choosing the most advanced model. It is about formulating a useful task, obtaining appropriate data, validating the system honestly, implementing it in the real workflow, and managing the risks that appear at every stage.
Students should work in small groups. Each group should fill in a simple AI project canvas with the following elements:
• problem and intended users,
   • AI task and prediction/output,
   • data sources and labels,
   • baseline and modelling approach,
   • evaluation and validation plan,
   • implementation and monitoring plan,
   • risk register and go/no-go decision points.
Encourage critical thinking. For each proposed AI project, students should ask: Is AI really needed? Is the target measurable? Is there enough data? Would a simpler baseline solve the problem? What could go wrong after deployment? Who is responsible if the system fails?
The output of the session should be a short project canvas or one-page project brief, not code. The teacher may provide a template before the lesson to keep group work focused.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce the aim of the session: how to move from an AI idea to a realistic AI project plan.
   • Present the running example and briefly describe the intended users, context, and expected benefit.
   • Explain that the session output will be an AI project canvas rather than a model or code.
10 - 25 minutes
• Discuss problem formulation: What real-world decision or workflow should improve? Who will use the system? What is the current non-AI process?
   • Distinguish the business/clinical/organizational problem from the machine-learning task.
   • Group activity: define the user, decision point, AI output, and success criterion for the case.
25 - 40 minutes
• Discuss project scope and feasibility: what is in scope, what is explicitly out of scope, and what would count as a useful first version.
   • Introduce baselines: manual process, rule-based system, simple statistical model, or existing software.
   • Group activity: define a minimal viable AI project and one simple baseline that must be beaten.
40 - 58 minutes
• Explain data collection and data access: available sources, ownership, privacy, consent, data quality, missingness, and representativeness.
   • Discuss labels and ground truth: where labels come from, how noisy they are, who creates them, and whether they encode bias or future information.
   • Group activity: create a data map listing inputs, target labels, sensitive variables, unavailable data, and likely data-quality problems.
58 - 72 minutes
• Discuss modelling strategy: start simple, build baselines, select features/representations, and only then consider more complex models.
   • Explain the difference between modelling experiments and production-ready implementation.
   • Group activity: choose a modelling path for the case: baseline, first model, possible advanced model, and criteria for moving to the next level.
72 - 88 minutes
• Discuss evaluation and validation: relevant metrics, uncertainty, calibration where needed, validation split, external or temporal validation, and subgroup checks.
   • Connect evaluation to intended use: a technically good metric is insufficient if it does not refle

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should introduce time series forecasting as a practical decision-support tool, not as a mathematically heavy modelling topic. The main aim is to help students understand what must be specified before a forecast is meaningful: what is being forecast, for whom, at what horizon, how often the forecast is updated, and what decision will be made from it.
Use one or two concrete running examples throughout the lecture, such as hospital bed demand, energy consumption, warehouse inventory demand, call-center workload, cloud computing capacity, public-transport passenger demand, or monthly project cost. Revisit the same example when discussing data structure, baselines, validation, uncertainty, and operational use.
The central intuition should be: forecasting is not just extrapolating a curve. It is a decision problem under temporal uncertainty. The right model depends on the horizon, data frequency, external drivers, cost of errors, and stability of the process.
Avoid turning the session into a catalogue of models. Mention model families only at a high level: naive and seasonal naive baselines, moving averages, exponential smoothing, ARIMA-like models, regression with lag and calendar features, tree/boosting models, and neural forecasting models. The emphasis should be on when these approaches are reasonable and how they should be validated.
Make temporal leakage explicit. Students should understand that random train-test splitting is usually inappropriate for forecasting because future information can leak into the past. Evaluation should mimic the real forecasting situation, for example with chronological splits or rolling-origin validation.
Connect forecasting to uncertainty and calibration. For demand, cost, and capacity planning, a point forecast is often insufficient; decision-makers usually need ranges, quantiles, or scenarios, because underestimation and overestimation may have asymmetric costs.
A good lecture arc is:
• why forecasting is needed in operational decisions,
   • what makes time series different from ordinary tabular prediction,
   • what patterns are commonly present in time series,
   • how simple and advanced forecasting models differ,
   • how forecasts should be validated and interpreted,
   • how forecasts are used for demand, cost, and capacity decisions.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce forecasting through familiar operational examples: demand for a product, expected project cost, hospital capacity, staff workload, or server load.
   • Define a time series as observations ordered in time, and define forecasting as predicting future values at a specified horizon.
   • Emphasize that a forecast is only useful if it supports a concrete future decision.
10 - 20 minutes
• Explain what must be specified in a forecasting problem: target variable, time unit, forecast horizon, update frequency, aggregation level, and intended use.
   • Discuss examples of demand prediction, cost estimation, and capacity planning, showing that the same data may support different forecasting tasks.
   • Explain that short-, medium-, and long-term forecasts may require different data and models.
20 - 30 minutes
• Introduce common time series patterns: trend, seasonality, weekday or calendar effects, cycles, noise, outliers, and sudden shocks.
   • Explain autocorrelation intuitively: nearby time points are often more similar than distant time points.
   • Show why time order matters and why randomly shuffling observations can destroy the structure of the problem.
30 - 40 minutes
• Present forecasting approaches at a high level: naive baseline, seasonal naive baseline, moving average, exponential smoothing, ARIMA-like models, regression with lag/calendar/external features, and machine-learning models.
   • Stress that simple baselines are not optional; they reveal whether a complex model adds real value.
   • Discuss when external variables may help, such as holidays, weather, prices, campa

The class is designed in two parts in between the students spend time on their own to solve the tasks assigned. The first half uses the slides IPE_1_Introduction.pptx.

(20-25 min) let the students try their first prompt, have them explore the interface and discuss the elements mentioned in the slides.
(25-30 min) Submit the assignment and give the students access to the slides IPE_1_assignments.pptx and the Excel Template Prompt Log.xlsx.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce the idea that a machine learning application is more than a model.
- Present a simple real-world example and ask what steps are needed before and after training.
- Define a learning system as an end-to-end pipeline from problem formulation to maintained use.
10 – 20 minutes
- Explain problem formulation: what is the prediction target, what is the unit of prediction, what inputs are available, and what success means.
- Show that different formulations of the same real-world problem may lead to very different systems.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain the data pipeline: data collection, preprocessing, labeling, splitting into train/validation/test sets, and the importance of preventing leakage.
- Introduce the idea that the quality of the system depends strongly on the quality and structure of the data.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain the model development stage at a high level: representation, model choice, training, and evaluation.
- Keep this generic and stress that the model is one component inside the larger system.
- Briefly connect to later LEs on supervised and unsupervised learning.
40 – 50 minutes
- Explain deployment and operation: batch vs real-time inference, integration into workflow, and the difference between offline evaluation and real-world use.
- Discuss typical deployment failures such as distribution shift and mismatched assumptions.
50 – 60 minutes
- Explain monitoring and maintenance: concept drift, performance degradation, retraining, feedback loops, and human oversight.
- Summarize the full pipeline and highlight common failure points.
- Final takeaway: designing a good learning system requires coherence across all stages, not only a good model.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce unsupervised learning with intuitive examples where labels are not available.
- Define unlabeled data and explain why discovering structure can still be useful.
- Contrast the setting with supervised learning.
10 – 20 minutes
- Introduce major unsupervised task types: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and representation learning.
- Explain what each task tries to achieve at a high level.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain clustering as grouping similar examples and discuss the idea of similarity and distance.
- Show that clustering results depend strongly on representation and assumptions.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain dimensionality reduction as compressing or visualizing data while preserving useful structure.
- Use simple examples to motivate why lower-dimensional structure may be helpful for exploration or preprocessing.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss anomaly detection and representation learning as other important unsupervised use cases.
- Emphasize that unsupervised methods often support downstream analysis rather than directly solving a final task.
50 – 60 minutes
- Discuss limitations and challenges: ambiguous outputs, sensitivity to representation, dependence on assumptions, and difficulty of evaluation.
- Summarize when unsupervised learning is useful and when results should be treated cautiously.
- Final takeaway: unsupervised learning is about discovering potentially useful structure, not recovering a single ground truth answer.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce supervised learning with intuitive examples.
- Define labeled data and the goal of learning from example input–output pairs.
- Explain why this setting is so common in practical machine learning.
10 – 20 minutes
- Introduce the two main supervised task types: classification and regression.
- Use simple examples to distinguish discrete outputs from continuous outputs.
- Show typical application domains for each.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain the basic workflow of supervised learning: training data, validation, test data, and prediction on unseen cases.
- Introduce the idea of generalization and why training accuracy alone is not enough.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain at a high level how supervised models learn patterns from data.
- Briefly mention model families such as linear models, decision trees, and neural networks, without going into technical depth.
- Emphasize that different models are different ways of approximating input–output relationships.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss key challenges: overfitting, noisy or incorrect labels, poor feature representation, class imbalance, and dataset bias.
- Show how a model may perform well during development but fail on new data.
50 – 60 minutes
- Summarize when supervised learning is appropriate and when it may be problematic.
- Revisit the running examples and identify the labels, the prediction target, and the likely limitations.
- Final takeaway: supervised learning is powerful when high-quality labeled data and a well-defined prediction task are available.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce NLP through familiar examples such as spam filtering, search, translation, or chatbots.
- Define NLP as the computational processing and analysis of human language.
- Explain why language is an important but difficult data type.
10 – 20 minutes
- Discuss core challenges of language: ambiguity, synonymy, polysemy, compositionality, context dependence, and variability across speakers and domains.
- Show why “understanding text” is harder than simple pattern matching.
20 – 30 minutes
- Introduce major NLP task families: text classification, sequence labeling, information extraction, machine translation, summarization, question answering, and dialogue.
- Use simple examples to distinguish these task types.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain how text can be represented computationally at a high level: tokens, features, bag-of-words, and embeddings.
- Emphasize that representation strongly affects what an NLP system can learn.
40 – 50 minutes
- Present the broad evolution of NLP approaches: rule-based methods, statistical methods, and neural methods.
- Briefly explain what each family contributes and where its limitations lie.
50 – 60 minutes
- Place modern LLMs within the NLP landscape as a recent and powerful development, without going into depth.
- Summarize what kinds of problems NLP can solve and where caution is needed.
- Final takeaway: NLP is the broader field of turning language into something computationally tractable, while preserving enough structure and meaning to support useful tasks.

Recommended reading:
Leijnen, S., Maathuis, H., van Montfort, K., van Otterloo, S., Sent, D., Stalenhoef, M., van Turnhout, K., & Zwaal, R. (2025). Guideline for user interface design of explainable AI. Utrecht University of Applied Sciences.

The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce the problem of black-box AI using a concrete scenario.
- Ask why people may demand explanations for AI-supported decisions.
- Define the lecture scope: explainability as a technical, ethical, and user-centered issue.
10 – 20 minutes
- Define and distinguish the core concepts: black box, interpretability, explainability, transparency, and traceability.
- Clarify where these concepts overlap and where they do not.
- Show that explainability is not the same as simply revealing the code or model structure.
20 – 30 minutes
- Discuss the technical dimension of explainability: model understanding, feature importance, local vs global explanations, faithful vs approximate explanations.
- Introduce feature importance as a common form of local explanation. Mention LIME and SHAP as widely used examples, but only conceptually. 
- Briefly contrast feature importance with other explanation types: counterfactual explanations, similar-case explanations, and rule-based explanations.
- Emphasize that technical explanations have limits: they may approximate the model, may be unstable, may be misunderstood by users, and do not by themselves guarantee fairness or accountability.
30 – 40 minutes
- Discuss the ethical and legal dimension: accountability, contestability, justice, responsible decision-making, and the often-invoked idea of a “right to explanation.”
- Explain that explanation may matter not only for understanding but also for challenging decisions and supporting procedural fairness.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss the user dimension: acceptance, understanding, usability, and the mismatch that can occur between expert-level and user-level explanations.
- Use the running example to show that different stakeholders need different kinds of explanation.
50 – 60 minutes
- Summarize strengths and limitations of XAI.
- Revisit the running example and ask: what kind of explanation is needed, for whom, and is it actually achievable?
- Final takeaway: explainability can support trustworthy AI, but it is not a complete substitute for validity, fairness, or accountability.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
•	Introduction: AI systems around us, examples of impressive AI systems capabilities (e.g., self-driving cars, robots performing surgery, AI art generators, etc.) – 10 min
•	Scientific (textbook) definitions of AI – 30 min
-	systems that think like humans
  -	systems that think rationally
  -	systems that act like humans
  -	systems that act rationally
•	Weak vs. strong AI: the concepts of Narrow (Weak) AI and General (Strong) AI – 20 min
•	Legal definitions of AI (EU AI Act, OECD Principles on AI, 15 U.S. Code § 9401, etc.) – 10 min
•	More about the philosophy of AI – 10 min
-	What is intelligence?
  -	Can machines think?
  -	Ethical implications of AI
  -	Metaphysics of AI
  -	Epistemology of AI
•	Basic AI concepts: problem solving and search, planning, knowledge representation and reasoning, machine learning, intelligent agents, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, ethics and bias in AI – 20 min
•	Main AI-related areas – 10 min
-	core AI disciplines 
  -	applied AI areas 
  -	AI-supporting technologies
  -	AI-related interdisciplinary fields
  -	emerging and advanced AI disciplines
•	Wrap up: what is and what is not AI – 10 min

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
•	Introduction: need for responsible human-centered AI systems – 10 min
•	Current fields of AI research – 40 min
-	the Gartner hype cycle for AI
  -	machine learning: deep learning, reinforcement learning, self-supervised learning, transfer learning, generative models 
  -	natural language processing (NLP): large language models, multimodal NLP, commonsense reasoning, text summarization and generation, machine translation
  -	computer vision: object detection and segmentation, image/video classification, generative vision models
  -	robotics: autonomous navigation, swarm robotics
  -	causal AI
  -	quantum AI
•	Modern applications of AI systems – 40 min
-	healthcare: medical diagnosis and treatment planning, drug discovery, predictive analytics, robotic surgery
  -	transportation: autonomous vehicles, traffic management, route optimization
  -	finance: fraud detection, credit scoring, personal financial advisors
  -	customer service: chatbots and virtual assistants, recommender systems
  -	security and defense: cybersecurity, surveillance and monitoring
  -	education: personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading
  -	agriculture: precision farming, crop monitoring, agricultural robotics
  -	environmental protection: climate modeling, wildlife conservation, pollution monitoring
•	Core principles of responsible AI – 30 min
-	fairness and non-discrimination
  -	transparency and explainability
  -	accountability and governance
  -	privacy and data protection
  -	reliability and safety
  -	human-centricity and oversight
  -	inclusivity and societal benefit
  -	environmental and economic sustainability
  -	legal and regulatory compliance
•	Existing regulatory frameworks for AI – 40 min
-	EU AI Act
  -	OECD Principles on AI
  -	US Executive Order 13859
•	Summary: analysis of possible scenarios for the development of AI – 20 min

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 - 10 minutes
- Introduce real-world examples of AI in healthcare (e.g., diagnosis, risk prediction)
- Motivate the need for AI in clinical decision-making
- Discuss why healthcare problems are fundamentally challenging (data quality, uncertainty)
10 - 35 minutes
- Explain the concepts of AI, machine learning, and deep learning
- Introduce supervised vs unsupervised learning
- Map learning paradigms to healthcare tasks (diagnosis, prognosis, patient stratification)
35 - 60 minutes
- Present main healthcare data types (EHR, imaging, time series, omics)
- Explain key characteristics (structure, dimensionality, noise, missingness)
- Interactive: students classify example problems into task types
60 - 80 minutes
- Introduce major model families (linear models, tree-based models, neural networks)
- Explain their assumptions and typical use cases
- Relate models to healthcare data modalities
80 - 100 minutes
- Explain evaluation concepts (train/test split, generalization, overfitting)
- Confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV, AUROC/AUPRC, calibration and threshold selection
- Discuss healthcare-specific challenges (class imbalance, label noise, dataset shift)
100 - 115 minutes
- Integrated healthcare mini-case: select a model and identify methodological flaws
- Interactive discussion: identify problems (bias, overfitting, poor validation)
- Emphasize limitations and risks of AI in healthcare
115 - 120 minutes
- Summarize key concepts (data -> task -> model -> evaluation -> limitation)
- Short Q&A
The healthcare mini-case:
A hospital develops a model for predicting a rare adverse event. Students receive the prevalence and confusion matrices for two models. They compare sensitivity, PPV and false positives, choose a deployment threshold, and discuss whether the model is suitable. They then learn that preprocessing occurred before the split, some patients appeared in both sets, and performance deteriorated at another hospital.
This single case covers:
- prevalence and PPV;
- model selection;
- threshold trade-offs;
- leakage;
- internal versus external validation;
- dataset shift;
- generalizability;
- clinician, developer and manager perspectives.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
When?

What?


First 30 minutes of the lesson

Introduction to omics data. Discuss the different types of omics data (metabolomics, proteomics, transcriptomics etc.) and the characteristics that make omics data special (batch effects, sparse data, high dimensionality (p >> n).

Short introduction of the RNA-sequencing case study and the RNA-sequencing data processing workflow (before the count table).



60 minutes of the lesson

Students work on a case study (count table of an RNA-seq experiment):

1.        The students shortly look at the mapping statistics and try to interpret them. 
2.        The students explore the raw count table (amount of zero values, library size [=total counts per sample], number of detected genes etc.) and the metadata.
3.        The students create a PCA plot and perform hierarchical clustering on the raw count table. The students draw conclusions. 
4.        The students perform log-transformation (log2(count + 1)) and redo the PCA/clustering/drawing conclusions.
5.        The students perform variance filtering and redo the PCA/clustering/drawing conclusions. 




Last 10 minutes of the lesson

Short wrap up for the lesson (conclusions + discussion point that all different forms of omics data have their own specific challenges).

wiki_sections.text:
Obligatory for students:
Read in advance (it is short): EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 25, Responsibilities along the AI value chain.
Optional for students:
Recommended (not mandatory) preceding LEs: LC-001 (AI Act and EU Digital Rulebook), LC-015 (Data Lifecycle Governance, for the provenance and lineage that vendor due diligence relies on), LC-034 (High-Risk Classification Workshop). Recommended for teachers:
Teachers should re-verify two fast-moving items before delivery: the status of the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (under appeal at the Court of Justice since October 2025) and the EU AI Act high-risk application date (deferred to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus), which governs when the Article 25 value-chain duties bite. See the notes in Lesson materials.

wiki_sections.name: Lesson materials
wiki_sections.text:
*European Commission, Standard Contractual Clauses for international data transfers, Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021 (the modular 2021 SCCs: controller-to-controller, controller-to-processor, processor-to-processor, processor-to-controller), and the Commission Q&A on the SCCs (25 May 2022). The Commission has additional SCC sets in development, including one for importers already directly subject to the GDPR.
Court of Justice of the EU, Case C-311/18 (Schrems II, 16 July 2020), which invalidated the Privacy Shield and requires a transfer impact assessment plus supplementary measures where the destination country's law does not offer essentially equivalent protection; European Data Protection Board, Recommendations 01/2020 on supplementary transfer tools.
European Commission, EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision (10 July 2023). Status note: the General Court upheld the decision in Latombe v Commission (T-553/23) on 3 September 2025, and Latombe appealed to the Court of Justice on 31 October 2025, so its future is not settled. The DPF is the third transatlantic mechanism after Safe Harbor (invalidated 2015) and Privacy Shield (invalidated 2020); re-verify status before delivery.
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 28 (processor obligations, and the duty to impose the same data-protection terms on sub-processors) and Article 46 (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards).
European Commission, EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 25 (responsibilities along the AI value chain: when a deployer, distributor, importer, or third party becomes a provider; the cooperation duty of the initial provider; the written-agreement duty toward third-party suppliers, with a carve-out for free and open-source components; and the AI Office task to publish voluntary model contractual terms), and Article 53 (obligations of general-purpose AI model providers, including documentation for downstream providers). Note on timing: the high-risk obligations were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus, and general-purpose AI obligations apply from 2 August 2025; re-verify before delivery.
Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), in force 17 January 2025: ICT third-party risk management, the register of information, the mandatory contractual clauses (Article 30), and the oversight of critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs). The European Supervisory Authorities designated the first 19 CTPPs in November 2025, spanning hyperscale cloud, data-centre, network, and financial-technology providers (a concrete picture of concentration risk).
ISO/IEC 27036 (information security for supplier relationships) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI management system), as the standards a vendor risk programme can be built and audited against.
On AI provenance: an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) extends the software bill-of-materials idea (SPDX, CycloneDX) to models, datasets, and components, so a buyer can see what is inside a third-party model. This ties back to LC-015 (Data Lifecycle Governance).
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 60-minute lecture makes one argument: when you buy or build on someone else's AI, you inherit their risk, and the contract is where you decide who carries it. The organising idea is that third-party vendor risk is managed through two contractual mechanisms and one regulatory allocation. The two mechanisms are Standard Contractual Clauses, which carry the data-transfer risk, and liability flow-down clauses, which carry the obligation and blame. The regulatory allocation is the EU AI Act value chain, which decides who counts as the provider and who counts as the deployer regardless of what the parties would prefer. Deliver it as a lecture with two short think-pair prompts where marked.
0 to 8 minutes: Framing and the vendor risk lifecycle
Open with the problem: almost no organisation builds its AI stack alone. It rents foundation models through an API, runs them on someone else's cloud, and passes data through sub-processors it has never audited. Every one of those relationships is a way for risk to enter that the organisation does not directly control.
Name why AI makes this worse than ordinary IT procurement: the model can be updated underneath you without notice, its training data and behaviour are opaque, and the market is concentrated on a handful of model and cloud providers, so a single failure or outage is felt everywhere at once.
Set out the vendor risk management lifecycle in one pass: due diligence before you sign, contracting to allocate the risk, monitoring while the relationship runs, and a clean exit when it ends. State the thesis: the rest of this lecture is about the contracting stage, because that is where the two mechanisms and the regulatory allocation do their work.
8 to 20 minutes: The data-transfer leg, Standard Contractual Clauses
Start with the trigger: the moment personal data leaves the EU or EEA to a vendor abroad, GDPR Chapter V applies, and the transfer needs a lawful basis. Standard Contractual Clauses are the Article 46 safeguard most vendors rely on.
Explain the 2021 SCCs: adopted by the Commission on 4 June 2021, they replaced the older clauses and are modular, with four modules for the controller-to-controller, controller-to-processor, processor-to-processor, and processor-to-controller relationships. You pick the module that matches the parties' roles and attach it to the contract.
Explain the post-Schrems II duty, because signing the SCCs is not enough. The Court of Justice held in Schrems II (2020) that the exporter must assess whether the destination country's law would undermine the clauses (a transfer impact assessment) and, where it would, add supplementary measures such as strong encryption. SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment plus supplementary measures is the working pattern.
Address the EU-US case directly, because students will ask. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (2023) lets certified US importers receive EU data without SCCs. Be honest about its status: the General Court upheld it on 3 September 2025, but that ruling was appealed to the Court of Justice on 31 October 2025, and this is the third such framework after two were struck down. Treat the DPF as usable today but not settled, which is exactly why the SCC fallback still matters.
20 to 32 minutes: The obligation leg, liability flow-down
Draw the distinction: SCCs move the data-transfer risk, but they do not decide who pays when the vendor causes a breach or the system causes harm. That is what flow-down does.
Walk the contractual toolkit and what each part is for: back-to-back (flow-down) clauses that push the obligations a buyer owes its own customers or regulators down onto the vendor; indemnities that shift the cost of specified failures; limitation-of-liability caps that the vendor will push to keep low and the buyer must resist for the risks that matter; and audit and step-in rights that let the buyer verify compliance and take over or remediate when the vendor fails.
Ground it in data protection with GDPR Artic

Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 33 and 34 (personal data breach notification: 72 hours to the supervisory authority, and communication to affected individuals where the risk to them is high); Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), incident reporting (24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification); Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), ICT-related incident reporting for financial entities. These are the parallel clocks that a single AI incident can start.
Trustworthy AI frameworks: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI 100-1), the seven trustworthiness characteristics (valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed); the EU High-Level Expert Group Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (the seven requirements) and the ALTAI self-assessment.
Trust in automation: Lee and See (2004), Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance; Parasuraman and Riley (1997), on misuse (over-trust) and disuse (under-trust), for the trust-calibration and trust-repair vocabulary.
Crisis communications: Coombs, Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT); Benoit, image repair theory; Arpan and Roskos-Ewoldsen (2005) on "stealing thunder"; Prahl and Goh (2021), "'Rogue machines' and crisis communication", on how AI-failure crises differ; Schneider et al. (2026) on the reputational cost of crisis responses attributed to AI (present as suggestive, from a single recent study).
Incident trackers for real cases: the OECD AI Incidents Monitor (oecd.ai), the AI Incident Database (incidentdatabase.ai), and the AIAAIC repository. Pull one or two current, verified cases from these rather than relying on a fixed example that may date.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute interactive session makes one argument: when your AI causes a public incident, you are running two clocks at once. There is a legal reporting clock (Article 73 and its cousins) and a reputational clock (the public response), and trustworthiness, once lost, is what you have to rebuild. Managing the crisis means coordinating both clocks so that neither the lawyers nor the communicators decide alone. The centre of the session is a crisis simulation; the lecture parts exist to arm the students for it.
0 to 10 minutes: Framing and the two clocks
Define the terms: an AI incident is any event where an AI system causes or nearly causes harm; a serious incident has the meaning given in Article 3(49) of the AI Act. Point students to the incident trackers (OECD AI Incidents Monitor, the AI Incident Database, AIAAIC) as the public record of what actually goes wrong.
Name why AI incidents are not ordinary product incidents: the system is opaque, so the organisation often cannot say quickly why it failed; harm happens at scale and speed; there is an accountability gap where "the algorithm did it" sounds like an excuse; people anthropomorphise the system; and a single screenshot goes viral before any statement is ready.
State the thesis: two clocks start at once. Preview them, then run the simulation against them.
10 to 25 minutes: The legal clock, the reporting web
Article 73: providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to the national market surveillance authority, on a tiered deadline measured from the moment they become aware and establish a causal link or its reasonable likelihood: no later than 2 days for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, 10 days where a person has died, and 15 days for other serious incidents. Article 72 requires a documented post-market monitoring system that feeds this.
The general-purpose track: for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, serious incidents are reported to the AI Office under Article 55, not through the market-surveillance route. This is the track that is already live.
The parallel clocks: one AI incident can be several legal events at once. If personal data is exposed, GDPR Articles 33 and 34 start a 72-hour clock to the supervisory authority and, where the risk is high, a duty to tell the affected people. NIS2 adds a 24-hour early warning and a 72-hour notification for essential and important entities; DORA adds ICT-incident reporting for financial firms.
The point that matters for communications: these deadlines are not optional and they are often shorter than the time the organisation would like to take before going public. The legal clock constrains the reputational one.
25 to 40 minutes: The reputational clock, trustworthiness and crisis communications
Trustworthiness is the asset a crisis destroys. Use the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's characteristics (valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed) and the EU trustworthy-AI requirements to name what the public believed about the system and what the incident has now put in doubt.
Give the trust vocabulary: trust guides reliance when a system is too complex to fully understand (Lee and See, 2004), and it fails in two directions, over-trust leading to misuse and under-trust leading to disuse (Parasuraman and Riley, 1997). A crisis is a trust-calibration event, and the job afterwards is trust repair.
Crisis-communication theory: Situational Crisis Communication Theory (Coombs) sorts crises by how much responsibility the public attributes to the organisation, and matches a primary response posture (deny, diminish, or rebuild) to that attribution, with bolstering as a supplementary set of strategies; image repair theory (Benoit) gives the menu of moves; and "stealing thunder" (Arpan and Roskos-Ewoldsen, 2005) shows that breaking

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture makes one argument: data lifecycle governance is the foundation of AI you can trust, and it matters more now that organisations run non-deterministic LLM systems in production. The organising claim is that reliability in these systems does not come from the model, which cannot be made repeatable, but from the governance around the data, and that governance has to hold across the whole life of the data, not at a single checkpoint. Deliver it as a lecture with two or three short think-pair prompts where marked.
0 to 10 minutes: Framing and the GIGO principle
Open with the problem: organisations are placing machine-learning and LLM systems into production, and the question is not whether the model is clever but whether the outputs can be trusted, evidenced, and defended.
State the governing idea: model and system quality is bounded by data quality (garbage in, garbage out). Governance is how an organisation keeps that bound high across the life of the data.
Preview the arc: the lifecycle, then lineage and provenance, then data quality, then how governance runs in pipelines, then the reliability problem in LLM systems, then the legal anchors.
10 to 25 minutes: The data lifecycle and governance across it
Walk the stages: creation and collection, ingestion, storage, processing and transformation, use and serving, archival, and deletion or retention.
At each stage, name the governance question: who owns it (owner, steward, custodian), what policy applies, what metadata is captured, and what control has to work.
Reference frameworks: DAMA-DMBOK as the management and governance body of knowledge, and the GDPR lifecycle principles (data minimisation, storage limitation, accuracy) as the legal version of the same discipline.
Think-pair prompt: pick one stage and name the single control whose failure would most damage trust in the final numbers.
25 to 40 minutes: Lineage and provenance
Define and separate the two. Lineage is the path data takes through systems and transformations (where a value came from and what it fed). Provenance is the record of origin, history, and responsibility for a thing (who and what produced it, so its quality and trustworthiness can be judged).
How lineage is captured: OpenLineage as the vendor-neutral open standard, modelling datasets, jobs, and runs, and supporting column-level lineage (which input columns produce each output column); Marquez as the reference implementation; and the role of data catalogs.
Provenance standards: W3C PROV-DM (Entity, Activity, Agent) as the general model; C2PA content credentials as the media-and-AI-generated-content version, with the honest caveat that credentials are designed to persist but are often stripped by platforms.
Why it matters: trust, audit, reproducibility, debugging, incident response, and regulatory evidence. Make the point that you cannot investigate a bad output you cannot trace.
40 to 52 minutes: Data quality and GIGO in practice
The dimensions of data quality: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness.
How poor quality propagates, and where: distinguish training data (quality bakes into the model) from inference-time or retrieved context (quality determines what a running LLM sees on each request). The failure modes and the controls differ.
Operational tooling to make quality testable: data-quality checks such as Great Expectations, dbt tests, and Soda; and dataset documentation such as datasheets for datasets and data cards.
52 to 64 minutes: Governance operationalised (MLOps and LLMOps)
The point: governance that lives in a policy document does not run; governance in a pipeline does. Show what that looks like in practice.
Data and prompt versioning (for example DVC and lakeFS for data; version control for prompts and evaluations), feature stores, drift monitoring, and dataset documentation as pipeline artefacts.
Frame this as extending the lifecycle view into running systems: the same lineage, provenance,

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 180-minute capstone workshop makes one argument: an AI governance handbook is not a binder of policies, it is the operating system that turns scattered legal obligations into controls an organisation actually runs and evidence it can show. The two ideas that hold it together are the policy artifact (a living, version-controlled, owned document that maps obligations to controls to evidence) and the integrated strategy (one operating model rather than a stack of disconnected documents). The point that makes it concrete: the EU AI Act itself mandates this, because Article 17 requires the quality management system to exist as written policies, procedures and instructions. The session is mostly hands-on team work; the taught parts exist to arm the build. Teams need a facilitator, a scenario each, and a blank register template.
0 to 15 minutes: Framing, the handbook as a policy artifact
Open with the reframe: everything in the Law and Compliance track was a piece of one thing. Data governance, high-risk classification, conformity assessment, technical documentation, vendor risk, and crisis management are not separate topics, they are sections of a governance handbook.
Define policy-as-artifact: a living document suite with a named owner, version control, and a review cadence, whose job is to map each obligation to a control and to the evidence that the control runs. Contrast it with policy theatre, a document written to be filed and never used.
Anchor it in law: Article 17 requires a provider of a high-risk system to run a documented quality management system, in written policies, procedures and instructions, covering the compliance strategy, change management, and post-market monitoring. The handbook is that system written down.
15 to 35 minutes: The method and the frameworks
Teach the through-line method: obligations to controls to evidence. For each legal obligation, name the control that satisfies it and the artifact that proves the control ran. This is what makes a handbook auditable rather than aspirational.
Give the two frameworks that supply the control vocabulary. ISO/IEC 42001, the AI management system standard, gives a Plan-Do-Check-Act structure and an Annex A control set (38 controls across nine areas, from policies through to third-party relationships). The NIST AI Risk Management Framework gives four functions, Govern, Map, Measure and Manage; it is voluntary and complements the AI Act rather than replacing it. Show that a cross-framework register lets a team line up an AI Act obligation, an ISO 42001 control, and a NIST function side by side so nothing is missed; a published crosswalk between the AI RMF and ISO 42001 is available (hosted on the NIST AI Resource Center) to start from.
Give the operating model: the three lines of defence adapted to AI, where the first line owns the risk, the second monitors and challenges it, and the third gives independent assurance to the board (Schuett, 2023). Make the accountability point: concentrate it, with clear ultimate ownership and a single point for the risk process, rather than splitting it until no one owns it. Present the benefits as conditional, and note that the third-line framing is debated.
35 to 45 minutes: Brief the deliverable and form teams
State the deliverable: each team builds a governance-handbook artifact for one organisation and one high-risk system (for continuity, reuse a scenario from LC-026 or LC-012, for example a hiring screener, a credit or benefits decision system, or a customer-facing assistant).
The artifact has four parts, built at four stations: an inventory entry with a risk tiering; an obligations-to-controls-to-evidence register for the system; a roles, RACI and three-lines assignment; and the living-document mechanics. Assign roles within each team so the work parallelises.
