wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute interactive session takes a system that has already been classified as high-risk (see LC-034) and works through how its provider demonstrates conformity before it reaches the market. The organising idea is that conformity assessment is the step between being classified as high-risk and being placed on the market: it is where the requirements in Articles 9 to 15 are shown to be met, evidenced, and CE-marked.
5 minutes: Framing
Recap: a system is high-risk (Annex III). What now? Conformity assessment is the procedure by which the provider demonstrates and documents that it meets the high-risk requirements before placing it on the market.
Make clear this is product-safety logic borrowed from the New Legislative Framework, not a new invention.
15 minutes: The procedure
The two routes under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI, a self-assessment against the requirements and the technical documentation, with no notified body) and third-party assessment (Annex VII, assessment of the quality management system and of the technical documentation, involving a notified body).
Which route applies: for Annex III point 2 to 8 systems (employment, education, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice and the rest) the route is internal control under Annex VI, with no notified body. For Annex III point 1 (biometrics) the picture is conditional: where the provider has applied harmonised standards or common specifications, it may use internal control under Annex VI; where it has not, or where those standards do not cover all the requirements, it must use the notified-body route under Annex VII. Tie this straight to the next point, because the standards gap decides it.
Harmonised standards and the presumption of conformity: a system built to a harmonised standard whose reference is cited in the Official Journal is presumed to meet the corresponding requirement (Article 40). Flag the live problem: those standards (CEN-CENELEC JTC 21) are not yet cited, so providers currently cannot rely on them and must demonstrate conformity directly against Articles 9 to 15 or via common specifications adopted by the Commission (Article 41). For biometrics this is what pushes a provider toward a notified body.
The artefacts produced: technical documentation (Annex IV), the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), the CE marking (Article 48), and registration in the EU database (Article 49). Tie these to the quality management system (Article 17) and to post-market monitoring (Article 72) as the ongoing obligations.
55 minutes: Case work
Case 1 (route selection, Annex III point 4): an AI system that screens and ranks CVs in recruitment.
* Tasks: confirm it is high-risk; determine the conformity assessment route; list the evidence the provider must hold.
 * Expected outcome: internal control under Annex VI, no notified body; technical documentation and declaration of conformity required.
Case 2 (route selection, Annex III point 1): a remote biometric identification system.
* Tasks: work through the conditional routing; identify that without cited harmonised standards the provider is pushed to the notified-body route under Annex VII; discuss when involving a notified body is prudent even where internal control is technically available.
Case 3 (the standards gap): a provider must demonstrate conformity in 2026 to 2027 while the harmonised standards are still in development.
* Tasks: explain what "presumption of conformity" would give the provider; decide how to demonstrate conformity in the absence of a cited standard (direct demonstration against Articles 9 to 15, or common specifications under Article 41); discuss the risk and cost this creates.
Case 4 (substantial modification): a provider places a system on the market, then materially retrains the model and changes its intended purpose.
* Tasks: determine whether a new conformity assessment is triggered under Article 43(4); identify what has to be re-documented.
15 minutes: Synthe

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
5 minutes: Introduction to workshop format
•	Briefly recap high-risk classification logic (assumed prior knowledge).
•	Case-based legal reasoning and structured qualification.
•	Explain workflow: short input → case analysis → plenary discussion.
10 minutes: Key Concepts Refresher (Targeted)
•	Annex III catalogue: sector-specific high-risk use cases (e.g. employment, law enforcement, education).
•	Filter conditions: exclusion where system does not pose significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights.
•	Intended purpose (as defined by provider).
•	Reasonably foreseeable misuse (objective standard).
•	NLF logic: harmonised conformity assessment and CE-marking framework.
40 minutes (or more): Case Work – examples:
•	Case Study 1 – Annex III Qualification
* Scenario: AI system used for CV screening in recruitment.
* Tasks for students:
  * Identify relevant Annex III category (employment).
  * Determine whether system qualifies as high-risk per se.
  * Discuss borderline issues (decision-support vs. decision-making).
* Expected outcome: classification as high-risk AI system.
•	Case Study 2 – Application of Filter Conditions
•
* Scenario: AI system ranking job applicants based on non-decisive recommendations.
* Tasks:
  * Apply filter conditions:
    * Does the system materially influence decisions?
    * Is there a significant risk to fundamental rights?
  * Evaluate whether exclusion from high-risk category is justified.
* Focus: Burden of proof and documentation requirements.
•	Case Study 3 – Intended Purpose and Misuse
* Scenario: AI tool marketed for educational support, later used for student performance evaluation.
* Tasks:
  * Identify divergence between intended purpose and actual use.
  * Assess reasonably foreseeable misuse.
  * Determine classification consequences.
* Key insight: classification depends on objective functional use, not only declared purpose.
•	Case Study 4 – NLF and Conformity Assessment
* Scenario: High-risk AI system integrated into a medical device.
* Tasks:
  * Identify applicable conformity assessment pathway.
  * Discuss role of notified bodies and harmonised standards.
* AI Act builds on existing product safety architecture (NLF).
5 minutes: Plenary Discussion and Synthesis
•	Compare classification outcomes across groups.
•	Highlight common errors:
* Over-reliance on provider statements
* Misapplication of filter conditions
•	Reinforce structured approach:
* Annex III applicability
* Filter conditions
* Contextual use and misuse
* Compliance implications

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 60-minute lecture makes one argument: technical documentation is the file that proves a high-risk AI system is compliant, and drafting it well is the compliance expert's core deliverable. The organising idea is that Annex IV is not a checklist but the structure of the argument a provider makes to a regulator, and that two of its parts carry most of the weight in practice: the system description and the logging. Deliver it as a lecture with two short think-pair prompts where marked.
0 to 8 minutes: Framing, what the documentation is for
Open with the point: technical documentation is the evidence file. Under Article 11, the provider of a high-risk system must draw it up before the system is placed on the market, keep it up to date, and make it demonstrate that the system meets the high-risk requirements.
Place it in the compliance lifecycle: the documentation is what the conformity assessment (LC-026) actually assesses, it is the basis for the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and the CE marking (Article 48), and it must be kept at the disposal of national authorities for ten years after the system is placed on the market (Article 18).
State the thesis: if the system is ever investigated, this file is the provider's defence. Drafting it is not clerical work, it is where compliance is proved or lost.
8 to 30 minutes: Annex IV element by element
Set the frame: Annex IV lists nine categories the documentation must contain, in order, "as applicable" to the system. Walk them.
Element 1, a general description of the system: intended purpose, the provider's name, the version and how it relates to previous versions, how it interacts with hardware and other software including other AI systems, firmware versions, the forms in which it is placed on the market (embedded in hardware, downloads, APIs), the hardware it runs on, product photographs where relevant, a basic description of the user interface, and the instructions for use for the deployer.
Element 2, a detailed description of the system's elements and its development process: the methods and steps taken to develop it, the design specifications and general logic, the system architecture and computational resources, the data requirements set out as datasheets (training methodologies and datasets used), the assessment of the human oversight measures (Article 14), any pre-determined changes, and the validation and testing procedures with dated and signed test logs, reports, and metrics, plus cybersecurity measures.
Elements 3 to 9, more briskly: monitoring, functioning and control, including capabilities, limitations, accuracy, and foreseeable unintended outcomes (element 3); why the performance metrics chosen are appropriate (element 4); the risk management system under Article 9 (element 5); the relevant changes made through the lifecycle (element 6); the harmonised standards applied, or where none are applied, a description of the solutions adopted to meet the requirements (element 7); a copy of the EU declaration of conformity (element 8); and the post-market monitoring plan under Article 72 (element 9).
Think-pair prompt: for a high-risk system your organisation buys rather than builds, which Annex IV elements can you not complete without information from the vendor? (This connects to LC-002.)
30 to 42 minutes: The system description in depth
Return to elements 1 and 2, because this is where most drafting effort goes and where most files are weak. The test is whether a competent outsider could understand what the system is, how it was built, and how it is meant to be used, from the document alone.
Make the level of detail concrete: a version and model identity that pins down exactly which artefact is documented, an architecture description that names the components and how data flows through them, and data requirements documented as datasheets so the provenance and lineage of the training data can be judged (this is the vendor-facing side of LC-015, and where an AI B

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Tool: Scopus/Web of Science database, VOSviewer (latest version). 
Note: This is a computer practice session. Students must have active Scopus/WoS institutional access and have VOSviewer pre-installed on their workstations.
Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The instructor displays a high-resolution VOSviewer map from a recent study in sociology or media. Prompt for students: What patterns do you observe? Discuss the semantics of the visualization: node size (frequency/impact), edge thickness (link strength), and color-coded clusters (thematic or social proximity). 
2.	Conceptual Briefing (10 min): Define bibliometrics and its role in systematic literature reviews and state-of-the-art mapping. Distinguish between descriptive bibliometrics (productivity metrics, citation counts) and science mapping (structural relationships and intellectual evolution). Introduce the specific networks to be built: Co-authorship (social structure) and Keyword Co-occurrence (intellectual structure). Define VOSviewer parameters: nodes, edges, total link strength, clusters, and the minimum occurrence threshold. 
3.	Technical Demo (5 min): Demonstrate advanced data harvesting: building a query using Boolean operators (AND, OR, LIMIT-TO) and exporting metadata in CSV or RIS formats with full bibliographical information. 
4.	Data Collection (15 min): Students work individually or in pairs to define a research niche. They select a topic within media/culture (e.g., algorithmic bias, digital disinformation, platform labor, or AI in journalism). Students refine their queries to achieve a manageable corpus (300–800 records) to ensure visual clarity. 
5.	Descriptive Analysis (10 min): Using the database’s built-in "Analyze Results" tool, students report on the distribution of publications by year, top journals, and leading geographic regions.
6.	Science Mapping Practice (25 min): Students import their data into VOSviewer. They must generate two distinct maps: a co-authorship network and a keyword co-occurrence map. 
7.	Interpretation & Reporting (15 min): Students draft a brief report summarizing the primary research clusters and identifying the most influential nodes (authors or concepts) based on link strength. 
8.	Reflection and Sharing (15 min): Selected pairs present their maps.
9.	 Wrap-up (5 min): Summarize the key concepts and allow time for final questions. Homework: run the same query in both Scopus and Web of Science. Compare the resulting VOSviewer maps: are the thematic clusters consistent across databases?

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Tools: NodeXL. Gephi
Note: Students can have Gephi/NodeXL pre-installed on their notebooks.
Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The "Network Turn" in Social Sciences. Why connectivity often matters more than individual content in the digital age
2.	Conceptualizing the network (15 min): actors (nodes), relations (edges/ties), and attributes. Taxonomies of ties: directed vs. undirected, binary vs. weighted.
3.	Foundational Concepts (15 min): Introduce basic graph terminology. Discuss seminal studies: Jacob Moreno’s Sociometry, Mark Granovetter’s "Strength of Weak Ties" (information diffusion), and Manuel Castells’ "Network Society" as it pertains to contemporary media structures.
4.	Micro-discussion (10 min): Collaborative Mapping. In pairs, students select a specific media ecosystem (e.g., a newsroom hierarchy, a Twitter/X discourse community, or a podcast network) and sketch a graph with 5–7 nodes. Presentation of maps: Address the ontological question - what constitutes an "actor" in a media network? (Users, hashtags, bots, or media outlets).
5.	Core Metrics (15 min): Quantitative Interpretation of nodes. Degree centrality: popularity and immediate reach. Betweenness centrality: control over information flow and brokerage. Closeness centrality: efficiency and speed of access to the whole network.
6.	Network-Level Properties: Explain density, diameter, average path length (small world phenomenon), and clustering coefficient as the macro-context for interpretation.
7.	Applied Exercise (15 min): Manual calculation. Students compute degree and betweenness for a provided 7-node graph (on whiteboard or handout). Compare manual results with software output (Gephi/NodeXL) to demystify algorithmic calculations.
8.	Advanced Topology (10 min): Social Structures in Media. Clusters & Modularity: Identifying echo chambers, filter bubbles, and polarized discourse. Structural Holes (Ronald Burt): The role of the "broker" as a bridge between disconnected audiences. Opinion leaders vs. Bridge-builders in the digital landscape.
9.	Case-Study Analysis (15 min): Analyzing a real-world media campaign graph (pre-processed in Gephi, based on a familiar socio-political context). Task: Identify at least two distinct clusters; locate a node occupying a structural hole (broker); identify the top two opinion leaders. Justify each finding with the appropriate metric. Small group work followed by a brief plenary session.
10.	Conclusion & Reflection (5 min): One-sentence synthesis: "The most significant insight I gained today regarding media space through the lens of SNA is..."Synthesize student responses into the three core learning outcomes to reinforce the day's curriculum.

Title

The Economics Of Disinformation: Clickbait And Ad-Tech


CODE

MC-100


Duration

90

Lesson Type

wiki_sections.name: Management information
wiki_sections.text:
Author Organisation 1

Real AI


Author Person 1

Tarry Singh, Tannistha Maiti


Author Organisation 2




Author Person 2




Reviewer Organisation

HAW


Reviewer Person




Status

Lesson plan: review
Learning Outcomes:
Explain the attention economy and why engagement diverges from accuracy: students can explain, from Simon's account of attention as the scarce resource, why platforms and publishers optimise for engagement, and can summarise the evidence that false news spread faster and wider than true news on Twitter (Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, 2018) together with the limits of that generalisation (Juul and Ugander, 2021).Describe how programmatic advertising works and how it funds disinformation: students can explain real-time bidding and the roles of ad exchanges and demand-side and supply-side platforms, and explain why automated, quality-blind placement sends advertiser money to low-quality made-for-advertising and disinformation sites.Describe the scale and follow the money: students can use current figures to state the size of the problem, including the wasted programmatic spend measured by the Association of National Advertisers (about 26.8 billion dollars, Q2 2025), and can follow one brand's advertising budget through to a disinformation publisher, identifying Google and the major exchanges as the largest single sources (Global Disinformation Index; NewsGuard).Analyse how generative AI has changed the economics: students can explain how generative AI lowers the cost of clickbait and enables AI content farms built to harvest programmatic revenue (NewsGuard has tracked these into the thousands since 2023), and can describe the brand-safety failure in which reputable brands' ads appear on such sites without the advertiser's knowledge.Evaluate the follow-the-money countermeasures and their limits: students can explain demonetisation as the leading response, defunding content rather than removing it, name the main actors (the Global Disinformation Index, Check My Ads, brand-safety initiatives), and assess why the approach is disputed and, since 2024, in retreat, with GARM closed and the Global Disinformation Index no longer rating individual sites, and why the opacity of the marketplace limits enforcement.Apply the EU regulatory frame to a communication decision: students can explain the relevant duties under the Digital Services Act and the Code of Practice on Disinformation, now a Code of Conduct under Article 45 and in effect since 1 July 2025, covering advertising transparency, recommender-system rules, and demonetisation commitments, and can use them to justify an ad-placement or brand-safety decision.
Learning Events to be completed before:
None.
Keywords:
Attention economy,Engagement optimisation,Programmatic advertising,Real-time bidding,Made-for-advertising sites,Ad-tech,Clickbait,Brand safety,Demonetisation,Global Disinformation Index,Digital Services Act,Code of Practice on Disinformation,

wiki_sections.name: Expected preparation
wiki_sections.text:
Obligatory for students:
Harvard Business Review (2023). Are Your Ads Funding Disinformation?MIT News (2018). Study: On Twitter, false news travels faster than true stories. (Plain-language summary of Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, 2018.)

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines disinformation as an economic system: the financial incentives of the attention economy, the ad-tech machinery that pays for engagement, and the way AI has lowered the cost of producing content optimised for clicks rather than accuracy. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats disinformation not only as a content problem but as a supply chain with money at every step. The guiding question is who pays for this, and how.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from the logic of the attention economy to the plumbing of programmatic advertising to the effect of generative AI, and then to the responses. It starts with Simon's account of attention as the scarce resource and the evidence that engagement and accuracy pull apart, using the Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (2018) study of false-news spread and its documented limits. It then explains how programmatic advertising works, through real-time bidding across exchanges and demand-side and supply-side platforms, and why automated placement, indifferent to site quality, routes advertiser money to made-for-advertising and disinformation sites, at a scale the Association of National Advertisers measures in the tens of billions of dollars. It shows how generative AI has turned this into an industrial process, with thousands of AI content farms built to harvest ad revenue, and how reputable brands end up funding them without knowing. It closes on the countermeasures and their limits.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to reason about the money behind information. Students learn to follow the flow of advertising revenue from a brand's media budget to a disinformation publisher, to name the actors and mechanisms at each step, and to judge the countermeasures honestly, including why demonetisation is politically fraught and why several of its main implementers have pulled back under legal and political pressure. They then apply the EU frame: the Digital Services Act and the Code of Practice on Disinformation, now a Code of Conduct under Article 45, which carries advertising-transparency, recommender-system and demonetisation commitments. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding where a brand's or an institution's advertising may run, how to set brand-safety and inclusion rules, and how to defend those decisions when the marketplace is opaque. The teaching aim is judgement about incentives: content moderation alone does not touch the business model, and changing what gets funded is a different and harder lever.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, the attention economy: attention as the scarce resource (Simon), engagement as the currency, and why optimising for engagement diverges from accuracy; the Vosoughi et al. (2018) evidence and its limits.
15 to 40, the ad-tech machine: real-time bidding, exchanges, demand-side and supply-side platforms; made-for-advertising sites; why automated placement ignores site quality; the scale of wasted spend (ANA).
40 to 60, generative AI as an accelerant: AI content farms built for ad revenue (NewsGuard tracking since 2023); how ad money reaches disinformation publishers, and how a brand's ads end up on those sites through opaque programmatic buying rather than by choice; Google and the major exchanges are the largest single sources.
60 to 75, responses and their limits: demonetisation and follow-the-money (the Global Disinformation Index, Check My Ads, brand-safety), why it is contested, and its retreat under pressure; the EU frame (the Digital Services Act and the Code of Conduct on Disinformation).
75 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students trace the ad-revenue path for a given disinformation or AI-content-farm site, then draft a brand-safety and ad-placement policy for a named advertiser or public institution, and defend it against the transparency limits of the mark

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines the psychology of synthetic media: how AI-generated video, audio, images, and text change what audiences trust, how they judge what is real, and how public communication works when any recording can be challenged as fake. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats synthetic media as a shift in the conditions of belief, not as a detection problem to be solved with a better tool. The lecture is built around the liar's dividend: once convincing fakes are common, the mere possibility of a fake lets a speaker dismiss authentic evidence as fabricated.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from definitions to cognition to consequences to practice. It first separates deepfakes from cheapfakes and other manipulations and establishes that audiences react to the claim made about a piece of content more than to the technique behind it. It then explains the cognitive mechanisms that make synthetic content believable or persistent: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning. It then turns to the effects that matter most for a communicator. Current evidence indicates that political deepfakes are not, on average, more persuasive than other forms of misinformation, but that they destabilise trust in news and institutions and can damage the reputation of the person shown even when audiences rate the clip as not credible. The liar's dividend is presented as the sharpest form of this problem, with the experimental evidence for it and the current debate about how far it reaches video.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to work in an environment where authenticity can no longer be inferred from the medium. Students examine how repetition, reliance on social media, and motivated reasoning shape belief, why credibility ratings understate the real harm of synthetic content, and how the liar's dividend is used to avoid accountability. They then build a practical response: a verification and disclosure workflow that relies on content provenance (C2PA content credentials) and plausibility-aware checking rather than on detection alone, that meets the transparency and labelling duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act, and that communicates uncertainty without pushing audiences into indiscriminate distrust. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding under time pressure whether to publish, label, or challenge a piece of media, and explaining that decision to an audience. The teaching aim is judgement: understanding what synthetic media does to an audience, and choosing communication practices that hold up when any single piece of evidence can be called fake.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, definitions and taxonomy: deepfakes, cheapfakes, generated audio, image and text; why the claim attached to content matters more to audiences than the production method.
15 to 35, cognition: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning; the finding that higher cognitive ability and heavy social-media use change exposure, not immunity.
35 to 55, consequences: epistemic destabilisation, trust erosion, and reputational damage below the threshold of belief; the liar's dividend, the evidence for it, and the open question of how far it reaches video.
55 to 70, practice foundations: the limits of detection and warnings (the continued-influence effect and reality apathy); the elements of a provenance-first response using C2PA content credentials, plausibility-aware verification, and Article 50 labelling.
70 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students draft a verification-and-disclosure workflow for a newsroom or communications team facing a suspected deepfake, or a genuine recording that a public figure has dismissed as fake, and name the liar's-dividend risk an

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Introduce the topic and explain its importance for organisational digital transformation
Explain that digital transformation is not only about introducing new technologies, but also about rethinking workflows, information flows, and the way value is created
Explain what process mapping and value-stream mapping are
Clarify the difference between simply describing a sequence of actions and analysing which stages actually create value for the user, client, or organisation
Show that a value stream includes operations, waiting time, information transfer, delays, and losses
Review the main elements of a process map and a value-stream map: start and end of the process, stages, actors, information flows, completion time, waiting, handoffs, and outputs
Explain how to document the current state of a process and why this is the basis for meaningful improvement
Explain how mapping helps identify problem areas, such as unnecessary steps, duplication of actions, repeated data entry, delays, gaps between units, and overdependence on manual work
Provide a short example of a process where digital transformation should begin with understanding the current state rather than immediately introducing a new tool
Explain how AI tools can support process and value-stream mapping
Discuss examples of using AI to summarise textual descriptions of a process, turn notes into a structured sequence of stages, identify recurring problems, group types of waste, and support initial analytical preparation for process mapping
Emphasise that AI can accelerate analysis, but it does not replace collective understanding of the workflow or professional judgement
Introduce the concepts of current-state and future-state mapping
Explain how the current-state map can be used to define desirable improvements, digital intervention points, new coordination patterns, and ways to reduce waste
Stress that the future state should not simply be “more digital”, but more logical, faster, clearer, and more value-oriented
Discuss criteria for evaluating process quality in the context of digital transformation, including speed, continuity, transparency, user convenience, reduction of waste, quality of information transfer, scalability, and digital support
Briefly review the risks of superficial transformation, when digital tools are placed on top of an inefficient process without real redesign
Practical activity.
Learners work in groups on a short workflow that requires digital transformation, for example document approval, request processing, internal application review, public service delivery, or information exchange between units
Each group should outline the current state of the process, identify value-adding and non-value-adding stages, detect waste or delays, and propose a future-state version of the process
Groups may use free digital whiteboards or simple visual tools to build the map
In addition, groups may use AI tools to organise the process description, summarise problem points, or generate an initial list of possible improvements
Hold short presentations of group results
Discuss which types of waste and inefficiencies were identified, how realistic the future-state design is, and how the proposed changes support digital transformation
Wrap up the lesson
Emphasise that process and value-stream mapping are practical tools of digital transformation, and that combining visualisation, team analysis, and appropriate use of AI supports more informed decisions about process improvement

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
1.	Introduce the topic by asking why a small AI prototype may look cheap but become expensive when scaled across the organisation. Explain that AI economics is about understanding the costs, benefits, and trade-offs involved in building, buying, and operating AI systems.
2.	Explain tokenomics as the cost structure of using generative AI systems through tokens. A token is a small unit of text processed by a model. Both input and output usually count towards cost. Longer prompts, larger documents, longer responses, repeated queries, and bigger context windows all increase cost.
3.	Clarify the main cost drivers:
(a) Input tokens: the text sent to the model.
(b) Output tokens: the text generated by the model.
(c) Model choice: larger or more capable models usually cost more.
(d) Context length: long documents or conversations increase processing cost.
(e) Frequency of use: repeated use across many users multiplies cost.
(f) Latency and performance requirements: faster or higher-reliability systems may cost more.
(g) Human review: many AI outputs still require checking, approval, or correction.
(h) Integration and governance: security, monitoring, compliance, maintenance, and vendor management add cost.
4.	Use a simple example. A chatbot that costs only a few cents per conversation may seem cheap. However, if thousands of employees use it daily with long prompts and long outputs, the monthly cost can become significant. The business case must consider unit cost, volume, value per use, and risk.
5.	Explain the difference between three levels of AI economics:
(a) Prototype economics: small-scale, experimental, and low usage.
(b) Production economics: high-volume, monitored, governed, integrated, and continuously improved.
(c) Enterprise economics: includes training, compliance, support, vendor management, security, change management, and long-term maintenance.
6.	Introduce a simple economic assessment framework:
(a) What task is the AI performing?
(b) How often will it be used?
(c) How many tokens are used per interaction?
(d) Which model is required?
(e) What is the cost per use?
(f) What human review is needed?
(g) What time, cost, or quality benefit is created?
(h) Does the benefit justify the operating cost at scale?
7.	Discuss ways to manage cost. These may include using shorter prompts, limiting unnecessary output, using smaller models for simpler tasks, caching repeated answers, summarising documents before analysis, routing complex tasks only to advanced models, and monitoring usage by team or use case.
8.	Emphasise that the cheapest model is not always the best choice. A cheaper model may produce lower-quality outputs, require more human correction, or create business risk. The goal is not simply cost reduction, but value-for-money.
9.	Suggested Classroom Activity.
Ask groups to choose one AI use case, such as customer support, document summarisation, legal review, internal knowledge search, coding support, or report drafting. Each group should define the AI task, expected number of users, frequency of use, likely input and output size, model choice, main cost drivers, expected business benefit, risks and hidden costs, and ways to reduce cost while preserving value.
10.	Closing Message.
AI tokenomics helps organisations understand the real cost of using generative AI at scale. Good AI economics connects technical design with business value, ensuring that AI systems are not only impressive but also sustainable and cost-effective.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should introduce adversarial attacks as a reliability and safety problem in machine learning, not as a practical hacking tutorial. The goal is that students understand why ML systems may fail under deliberate manipulation, what kinds of failures are possible, and how this changes evaluation and deployment thinking.
Use intuitive examples throughout, such as a slightly modified image that fools a classifier, a spam email rewritten to bypass detection, fraudulent transactions shaped to look normal, poisoned training examples, or a user prompt designed to make an AI assistant ignore instructions. Keep examples conceptual and avoid step-by-step attack recipes.
The central intuition should be: a model can perform well on ordinary test data and still be fragile when inputs are chosen by an adaptive adversary. Standard accuracy is therefore not enough when a system is deployed in an environment where someone has an incentive to make it fail.
A good lecture arc is:
• what adversarial attacks are and why they matter,
   • how adversarial examples differ from ordinary errors,
   • what broad attack surfaces exist in the ML lifecycle,
   • why modern ML models can be vulnerable,
   • how adversarial risk should influence validation, monitoring, and deployment.
Keep the mathematical and algorithmic details light. It is acceptable to mention perturbations, decision boundaries, gradients, and high-dimensional spaces at an intuitive level, but do not teach attack algorithms in detail. The lecture should stay appropriate for a mixed-background horizontal audience.
Make the difference between accidental distribution shift and adversarial manipulation explicit. Both can cause failures, but adversarial settings are harder because the data-generating process reacts to the deployed system.
End with a balanced message. Adversarial robustness cannot usually be guaranteed absolutely, but threat modelling, appropriate testing, monitoring, secure data pipelines, and human oversight can reduce risk substantially.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce adversarial attacks using simple scenarios: a manipulated image classifier, a spam filter bypass, fraud detection, or a malicious prompt to an AI assistant.
   • Define an adversarial attack as an intentional attempt to make a machine learning system produce an incorrect, unsafe, or unintended output.
   • Contrast adversarial failures with ordinary model errors and random noise.
10 - 20 minutes
• Explain why standard test performance may be misleading when future inputs are chosen by an adaptive adversary.
   • Introduce the idea of a threat model: who can attack, what they can observe, what they can change, and what they want to achieve.
   • Discuss common goals of attackers: misclassification, bypassing detection, causing denial of service, extracting information, or manipulating downstream decisions.
20 - 30 minutes
• Present the main attack surfaces across the ML lifecycle: training data, feature pipeline, model interface, input data at inference time, outputs, and feedback loops.
   • Differentiate high-level attack types: evasion at inference time, data poisoning during training, model extraction, membership or privacy inference, and prompt or input manipulation in AI systems.
   • Use examples to show that attacks are not limited to images; they can affect text, tabular data, signals, recommender systems, and operational workflows.
30 - 40 minutes
• Explain intuitively why adversarial vulnerability can occur: high-dimensional inputs, brittle decision boundaries, shortcut learning, overconfidence, spurious correlations, and mismatch between training and deployment.
   • Discuss how small changes can be irrelevant to a human but important to a model, or alternatively realistic changes can exploit known model shortcuts.
   • Connect adversarial vulnerability to the broader themes of robustness, validation, and uncertainty.
40 - 50 minutes
• Discuss consequences

H-128
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should give students a compact statistical intuition for why numerical results and model predictions are never exact. It should not become a mathematical statistics course. The emphasis is on interpretation, communication, and decision-making under uncertainty.
Use one running example throughout, such as a medical risk prediction model, a loan default model, or a quality-control classifier. Revisit the same example when explaining estimates, confidence intervals, predicted probabilities, calibration, and threshold-based decisions.
The key intuition should be: statistical results are summaries of imperfect evidence. Good statistical reasoning asks not only “what is the number?”, but also “how uncertain is it?”, “what population does it apply to?”, and “can the predicted probabilities be trusted?”
A useful lecture arc is:
• why uncertainty appears even in clean-looking datasets,
   • how samples lead to estimates rather than exact truths,
   • how uncertainty can be quantified and visualized,
   • why probabilistic predictions need calibration,
   • and why calibrated probabilities matter for responsible decisions.
Keep formulas minimal. A simple mean/proportion, a confidence interval, and a reliability diagram are enough. Avoid deep derivations of probability theory, Bayesian inference, asymptotic theory, or advanced scoring rules.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce uncertainty through a familiar decision problem: e.g. a model says a patient has 20% risk, or a study reports that treatment A is better than treatment B.
   • Ask what would make the number trustworthy or misleading.
   • Define the lecture scope: uncertainty in data, estimates, predictions, and decisions.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explain sources of uncertainty: sampling variability, measurement error, missing data, label noise, population heterogeneity, and model assumptions.
   • Distinguish variability in the world from uncertainty in our knowledge about the world.
   • Use small examples to show why two samples from the same population can give different results.
25 - 40 minutes
• Introduce estimates, standard error, confidence intervals, and the idea that a result is a range of plausible values rather than a single exact value.
   • Clarify common misinterpretations: a confidence interval is not a guarantee for one individual, and statistical significance is not the same as practical importance.
   • Briefly compare uncertainty for a mean/proportion with uncertainty for a model performance metric.
40 - 55 minutes
• Explain prediction uncertainty: why a model output may be uncertain even if the fitted model is fixed.
   • Distinguish confidence intervals around an average effect from prediction intervals or predicted probabilities for individual cases.
   • Connect uncertainty to classification thresholds and the cost of false positives and false negatives.
55 - 70 minutes
• Introduce probabilistic predictions and calibration: among cases predicted as 20% risk, roughly 20% should experience the event.
   • Distinguish calibration from discrimination: a model can rank cases well but still produce overconfident or underconfident probabilities.
   • Introduce reliability diagrams/calibration curves, Brier score, and log loss at an intuitive level.
70 - 82 minutes
• Discuss miscalibration under dataset shift, subgroup differences, small samples, and overfitting.
   • Explain why recalibration may be necessary before deployment in a new population.
   • Use the running example to show how the same AUROC can support very different decisions depending on calibration.
82 - 90 minutes
• Summarize the practical checklist: What is the target population? How uncertain is the estimate? Are the probabilities calibrated? What decision threshold is used? What happens if the estimate is wrong?
   • Final takeaway: statistics is not a way to remove uncertainty; it is a way to make uncertainty visible, interpretable, and usable.

H-129

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should present robustness and validation as the “reality check” part of statistics and machine learning. The central question is not whether a result can be obtained, but whether it survives when we change the sample, assumptions, preprocessing, validation split, metric, or deployment context.
Use one running example throughout, ideally the same type of example used in H_128: a medical risk prediction model, a credit-risk model, or a quality-control model. Show how the model may look good during development but fail when evaluated on genuinely new data or a different subgroup.
The key intuition should be: a result is more credible when it is stable under reasonable perturbations and tested against data that were not used, directly or indirectly, to build it.
A useful lecture arc is:
• generalization as the goal of validation,
   • why train/test separation is necessary but not sufficient,
   • how leakage and repeated information create false confidence,
   • how external and subgroup validation reveal fragility,
   • and how robustness checks complement formal metrics.
Keep the lecture practical. Students should leave with a validation checklist they can apply to AI papers, projects, and deployed systems. Avoid spending too much time on the mathematics of resampling; focus on what each validation design can and cannot prove.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce a failure scenario: a model performs very well in development but fails in another hospital, another year, another device, or another user group.
   • Define validation and robustness in plain language.
   • Connect back to H_128: uncertainty tells us how precise evidence appears; validation asks whether the evidence travels.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explain generalization and the difference between training performance and performance on genuinely new cases.
   • Introduce overfitting as learning patterns that do not repeat.
   • Distinguish model development, model selection, and final evaluation.
25 - 40 minutes
• Explain train-validation-test splits, cross-validation, and why the final test set should be touched only once.
   • Discuss when random splits are reasonable and when grouped, temporal, patient-level, site-level, or geographical splits are needed.
   • Emphasize that the split must match the intended future use of the system.
40 - 55 minutes
• Discuss common validation failures: leakage, duplicated patients, preprocessing before splitting, target leakage, hyperparameter tuning on the test set, and labels that encode future information.
   • Use examples where leakage produces impressive but meaningless performance.
   • Give students a practical leakage-detection checklist.
55 - 68 minutes
• Explain metric choice and metric uncertainty: AUROC, accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, calibration metrics, and confidence intervals around performance.
   • Connect metrics to decision context: class imbalance, asymmetric costs, and threshold-dependent behavior.
   • Stress that no single metric validates a system.
68 - 80 minutes
• Introduce external validation, temporal validation, and subgroup validation.
   • Discuss distribution shift and why a model can fail without any coding error.
   • Use the running example to show how performance can differ across sites, devices, demographic groups, or time periods.
80 - 90 minutes
• Introduce robustness checks: sensitivity analyses, alternative preprocessing choices, baseline comparisons, ablations, negative controls, perturbation tests, and stress tests.
   • Summarize a validation report structure: data split, leakage prevention, metrics with uncertainty, subgroup/external validation, robustness checks, and known limitations.
   • Final takeaway: validation is not a ceremonial test at the end; it is the design logic that tells us whether a result deserves trust.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This practical should convert the ideas from H_128 and H_129 into a small but complete statistical workflow. Students should work with a prepared dataset and a prepared notebook or spreadsheet template, so the session is about reasoning rather than debugging.
Use a simple binary prediction task with predicted probabilities. Suitable examples include a synthetic medical risk dataset, loan default, equipment failure, readmission risk, or quality-control defect prediction. The dataset should include at least one grouping variable, such as site, year, device, hospital, user group, or demographic subgroup, so that validation and robustness can be demonstrated.
A Python notebook with pre-written helper functions is recommended: students should edit only a few lines, interpret plots, and fill in short conclusions.
The key intuition should be: statistical practice is an iterative chain of questions. What is the estimate? How uncertain is it? Are the predicted probabilities calibrated? Does the result survive a different split or subgroup? What would we report honestly?
The teacher should avoid turning the session into a programming exercise. Provide working code for data loading, plotting, and model fitting. The main student activity should be interpretation, comparison, and critical evaluation.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce the dataset, prediction target, variables, and intended decision context.
   • Clarify the output expected from students: a short statistical report or worksheet with plots, metrics, and conclusions.
   • Remind students of the H_128/H_129 checklist: uncertainty, calibration, validation, robustness.
10 - 25 minutes
• Explore the data: sample size, outcome prevalence, missingness, subgroup/site/year composition, and basic descriptive statistics.
   • Ask students to identify what the unit of analysis is and what future population the result should apply to.
   • Discuss whether a random split would be appropriate or whether grouped/temporal validation would be more realistic.
25 - 45 minutes
• Compute simple uncertainty summaries: confidence interval or bootstrap interval for outcome prevalence and one performance metric.
   • Compare a point estimate with its interval and discuss what the interval changes in the interpretation.
   • Ask students to write one cautious sentence that reports the estimate with uncertainty.
45 - 65 minutes
• Fit or load a simple probabilistic model, such as logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, or gradient boosting model.
   • Evaluate discrimination using AUROC or a similar ranking metric.
   • Compare training and test performance and identify signs of overfitting or overly optimistic evaluation.
65 - 82 minutes
• Construct a calibration curve or reliability table from predicted probabilities.
   • Compute or inspect Brier score/log loss and compare this with AUROC.
   • Discuss cases where the model ranks well but gives poorly calibrated probabilities.
82 - 98 minutes
• Explore threshold-based decisions: choose one threshold and compute sensitivity, specificity, false positives, and false negatives.
   • Discuss how the “best” threshold depends on the cost of mistakes and the use context.
   • Ask students whether the same threshold would be acceptable for all subgroups.
98 - 112 minutes
• Run at least two robustness checks: alternative random seed/split, subgroup evaluation, temporal/site holdout, missing-data perturbation, or comparison with a simple baseline.
   • Record which conclusions are stable and which change.
   • Discuss whether observed instability is random noise, real heterogeneity, or a validation-design problem.
112 - 120 minutes
• Students write a short conclusion: main result, uncertainty, calibration, validation design, robustness findings, and limitations.
   • Brief group discussion: what would be needed before using the model in practice?
   • Final takeaway: practical statistics is not the production of one met

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This interactive session should teach students how an AI project is normally structured in practice. It should not be a deep technical lesson about algorithms, nor a generic project-management lecture. The focus is the bridge between an AI idea and a working, validated, maintainable system.
Use one running case throughout the session, preferably a realistic but simple project such as medical risk prediction, customer-support email triage, predictive maintenance, document classification, or demand forecasting. The same case should be revisited from multiple angles: stakeholders, data, labels, baseline, model, validation, deployment, monitoring, and risks.
The central intuition should be: a successful AI project is not mainly about choosing the most advanced model. It is about formulating a useful task, obtaining appropriate data, validating the system honestly, implementing it in the real workflow, and managing the risks that appear at every stage.
Students should work in small groups. Each group should fill in a simple AI project canvas with the following elements:
• problem and intended users,
   • AI task and prediction/output,
   • data sources and labels,
   • baseline and modelling approach,
   • evaluation and validation plan,
   • implementation and monitoring plan,
   • risk register and go/no-go decision points.
Encourage critical thinking. For each proposed AI project, students should ask: Is AI really needed? Is the target measurable? Is there enough data? Would a simpler baseline solve the problem? What could go wrong after deployment? Who is responsible if the system fails?
The output of the session should be a short project canvas or one-page project brief, not code. The teacher may provide a template before the lesson to keep group work focused.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce the aim of the session: how to move from an AI idea to a realistic AI project plan.
   • Present the running example and briefly describe the intended users, context, and expected benefit.
   • Explain that the session output will be an AI project canvas rather than a model or code.
10 - 25 minutes
• Discuss problem formulation: What real-world decision or workflow should improve? Who will use the system? What is the current non-AI process?
   • Distinguish the business/clinical/organizational problem from the machine-learning task.
   • Group activity: define the user, decision point, AI output, and success criterion for the case.
25 - 40 minutes
• Discuss project scope and feasibility: what is in scope, what is explicitly out of scope, and what would count as a useful first version.
   • Introduce baselines: manual process, rule-based system, simple statistical model, or existing software.
   • Group activity: define a minimal viable AI project and one simple baseline that must be beaten.
40 - 58 minutes
• Explain data collection and data access: available sources, ownership, privacy, consent, data quality, missingness, and representativeness.
   • Discuss labels and ground truth: where labels come from, how noisy they are, who creates them, and whether they encode bias or future information.
   • Group activity: create a data map listing inputs, target labels, sensitive variables, unavailable data, and likely data-quality problems.
58 - 72 minutes
• Discuss modelling strategy: start simple, build baselines, select features/representations, and only then consider more complex models.
   • Explain the difference between modelling experiments and production-ready implementation.
   • Group activity: choose a modelling path for the case: baseline, first model, possible advanced model, and criteria for moving to the next level.
72 - 88 minutes
• Discuss evaluation and validation: relevant metrics, uncertainty, calibration where needed, validation split, external or temporal validation, and subgroup checks.
   • Connect evaluation to intended use: a technically good metric is insufficient if it does not refle

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This lecture should introduce time series forecasting as a practical decision-support tool, not as a mathematically heavy modelling topic. The main aim is to help students understand what must be specified before a forecast is meaningful: what is being forecast, for whom, at what horizon, how often the forecast is updated, and what decision will be made from it.
Use one or two concrete running examples throughout the lecture, such as hospital bed demand, energy consumption, warehouse inventory demand, call-center workload, cloud computing capacity, public-transport passenger demand, or monthly project cost. Revisit the same example when discussing data structure, baselines, validation, uncertainty, and operational use.
The central intuition should be: forecasting is not just extrapolating a curve. It is a decision problem under temporal uncertainty. The right model depends on the horizon, data frequency, external drivers, cost of errors, and stability of the process.
Avoid turning the session into a catalogue of models. Mention model families only at a high level: naive and seasonal naive baselines, moving averages, exponential smoothing, ARIMA-like models, regression with lag and calendar features, tree/boosting models, and neural forecasting models. The emphasis should be on when these approaches are reasonable and how they should be validated.
Make temporal leakage explicit. Students should understand that random train-test splitting is usually inappropriate for forecasting because future information can leak into the past. Evaluation should mimic the real forecasting situation, for example with chronological splits or rolling-origin validation.
Connect forecasting to uncertainty and calibration. For demand, cost, and capacity planning, a point forecast is often insufficient; decision-makers usually need ranges, quantiles, or scenarios, because underestimation and overestimation may have asymmetric costs.
A good lecture arc is:
• why forecasting is needed in operational decisions,
   • what makes time series different from ordinary tabular prediction,
   • what patterns are commonly present in time series,
   • how simple and advanced forecasting models differ,
   • how forecasts should be validated and interpreted,
   • how forecasts are used for demand, cost, and capacity decisions.
Suggested lesson structure
When?
What?
0 - 10 minutes
• Introduce forecasting through familiar operational examples: demand for a product, expected project cost, hospital capacity, staff workload, or server load.
   • Define a time series as observations ordered in time, and define forecasting as predicting future values at a specified horizon.
   • Emphasize that a forecast is only useful if it supports a concrete future decision.
10 - 20 minutes
• Explain what must be specified in a forecasting problem: target variable, time unit, forecast horizon, update frequency, aggregation level, and intended use.
   • Discuss examples of demand prediction, cost estimation, and capacity planning, showing that the same data may support different forecasting tasks.
   • Explain that short-, medium-, and long-term forecasts may require different data and models.
20 - 30 minutes
• Introduce common time series patterns: trend, seasonality, weekday or calendar effects, cycles, noise, outliers, and sudden shocks.
   • Explain autocorrelation intuitively: nearby time points are often more similar than distant time points.
   • Show why time order matters and why randomly shuffling observations can destroy the structure of the problem.
30 - 40 minutes
• Present forecasting approaches at a high level: naive baseline, seasonal naive baseline, moving average, exponential smoothing, ARIMA-like models, regression with lag/calendar/external features, and machine-learning models.
   • Stress that simple baselines are not optional; they reveal whether a complex model adds real value.
   • Discuss when external variables may help, such as holidays, weather, prices, campa

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce the idea that a machine learning application is more than a model.
- Present a simple real-world example and ask what steps are needed before and after training.
- Define a learning system as an end-to-end pipeline from problem formulation to maintained use.
10 – 20 minutes
- Explain problem formulation: what is the prediction target, what is the unit of prediction, what inputs are available, and what success means.
- Show that different formulations of the same real-world problem may lead to very different systems.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain the data pipeline: data collection, preprocessing, labeling, splitting into train/validation/test sets, and the importance of preventing leakage.
- Introduce the idea that the quality of the system depends strongly on the quality and structure of the data.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain the model development stage at a high level: representation, model choice, training, and evaluation.
- Keep this generic and stress that the model is one component inside the larger system.
- Briefly connect to later LEs on supervised and unsupervised learning.
40 – 50 minutes
- Explain deployment and operation: batch vs real-time inference, integration into workflow, and the difference between offline evaluation and real-world use.
- Discuss typical deployment failures such as distribution shift and mismatched assumptions.
50 – 60 minutes
- Explain monitoring and maintenance: concept drift, performance degradation, retraining, feedback loops, and human oversight.
- Summarize the full pipeline and highlight common failure points.
- Final takeaway: designing a good learning system requires coherence across all stages, not only a good model.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce unsupervised learning with intuitive examples where labels are not available.
- Define unlabeled data and explain why discovering structure can still be useful.
- Contrast the setting with supervised learning.
10 – 20 minutes
- Introduce major unsupervised task types: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and representation learning.
- Explain what each task tries to achieve at a high level.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain clustering as grouping similar examples and discuss the idea of similarity and distance.
- Show that clustering results depend strongly on representation and assumptions.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain dimensionality reduction as compressing or visualizing data while preserving useful structure.
- Use simple examples to motivate why lower-dimensional structure may be helpful for exploration or preprocessing.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss anomaly detection and representation learning as other important unsupervised use cases.
- Emphasize that unsupervised methods often support downstream analysis rather than directly solving a final task.
50 – 60 minutes
- Discuss limitations and challenges: ambiguous outputs, sensitivity to representation, dependence on assumptions, and difficulty of evaluation.
- Summarize when unsupervised learning is useful and when results should be treated cautiously.
- Final takeaway: unsupervised learning is about discovering potentially useful structure, not recovering a single ground truth answer.

0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce supervised learning with intuitive examples.
- Define labeled data and the goal of learning from example input–output pairs.
- Explain why this setting is so common in practical machine learning.
10 – 20 minutes
- Introduce the two main supervised task types: classification and regression.
- Use simple examples to distinguish discrete outputs from continuous outputs.
- Show typical application domains for each.
20 – 30 minutes
- Explain the basic workflow of supervised learning: training data, validation, test data, and prediction on unseen cases.
- Introduce the idea of generalization and why training accuracy alone is not enough.
30 – 40 minutes
- Explain at a high level how supervised models learn patterns from data.
- Briefly mention model families such as linear models, decision trees, and neural networks, without going into technical depth.
- Emphasize that different models are different ways of approximating input–output relationships.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss key challenges: overfitting, noisy or incorrect labels, poor feature representation, class imbalance, and dataset bias.
- Show how a model may perform well during development but fail on new data.
50 – 60 minutes
- Summarize when supervised learning is appropriate and when it may be problematic.
- Revisit the running examples and identify the labels, the prediction target, and the likely limitations.
- Final takeaway: supervised learning is powerful when high-quality labeled data and a well-defined prediction task are available.

- Explain why language is an important but difficult data type.
10 – 20 minutes
- Discuss core challenges of language: ambiguity, synonymy, polysemy, compositionality, context dependence, and variability across speakers and domains.
- Show why “understanding text” is harder than simple pattern matching.

- Explain how text can be represented computationally at a high level: tokens, features, bag-of-words, and embeddings.
- Emphasize that representation strongly affects what an NLP system can learn.

- Present the broad evolution of NLP approaches: rule-based methods, statistical methods, and neural methods.
- Briefly explain what each family contributes and where its limitations lie.
50 – 60 minutes
- Place modern LLMs within the NLP landscape as a recent and powerful development, without going into depth.
- Summarize what kinds of problems NLP can solve and where caution is needed.
- Final takeaway: NLP is the broader field of turning language into something computationally tractable, while preserving enough structure and meaning to support useful tasks.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 – 10 minutes
- Introduce the problem of black-box AI using a concrete scenario.
- Ask why people may demand explanations for AI-supported decisions.
- Define the lecture scope: explainability as a technical, ethical, and user-centered issue.
10 – 20 minutes
- Define and distinguish the core concepts: black box, interpretability, explainability, transparency, and traceability.
- Clarify where these concepts overlap and where they do not.
- Show that explainability is not the same as simply revealing the code or model structure.
20 – 30 minutes
- Discuss the technical dimension of explainability: model understanding, feature importance, local vs global explanations, faithful vs approximate explanations.
- Introduce feature importance as a common form of local explanation. Mention LIME and SHAP as widely used examples, but only conceptually. 
- Briefly contrast feature importance with other explanation types: counterfactual explanations, similar-case explanations, and rule-based explanations.
- Emphasize that technical explanations have limits: they may approximate the model, may be unstable, may be misunderstood by users, and do not by themselves guarantee fairness or accountability.
30 – 40 minutes
- Discuss the ethical and legal dimension: accountability, contestability, justice, responsible decision-making, and the often-invoked idea of a “right to explanation.”
- Explain that explanation may matter not only for understanding but also for challenging decisions and supporting procedural fairness.
40 – 50 minutes
- Discuss the user dimension: acceptance, understanding, usability, and the mismatch that can occur between expert-level and user-level explanations.
- Use the running example to show that different stakeholders need different kinds of explanation.
50 – 60 minutes
- Summarize strengths and limitations of XAI.
- Revisit the running example and ask: what kind of explanation is needed, for whom, and is it actually achievable?
- Final takeaway: explainability can support trustworthy AI, but it is not a complete substitute for validity, fairness, or accountability.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 - 10 minutes
- Introduce real-world examples of AI in healthcare (e.g., diagnosis, risk prediction)
- Motivate the need for AI in clinical decision-making
- Discuss why healthcare problems are fundamentally challenging (data quality, uncertainty)
10 - 35 minutes
- Explain the concepts of AI, machine learning, and deep learning
- Introduce supervised vs unsupervised learning
- Map learning paradigms to healthcare tasks (diagnosis, prognosis, patient stratification)
35 - 60 minutes
- Present main healthcare data types (EHR, imaging, time series, omics)
- Explain key characteristics (structure, dimensionality, noise, missingness)
- Interactive: students classify example problems into task types
60 - 80 minutes
- Introduce major model families (linear models, tree-based models, neural networks)
- Explain their assumptions and typical use cases
- Relate models to healthcare data modalities
80 - 100 minutes
- Explain evaluation concepts (train/test split, generalization, overfitting)
- Confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV, AUROC/AUPRC, calibration and threshold selection
- Discuss healthcare-specific challenges (class imbalance, label noise, dataset shift)
100 - 115 minutes
- Integrated healthcare mini-case: select a model and identify methodological flaws
- Interactive discussion: identify problems (bias, overfitting, poor validation)
- Emphasize limitations and risks of AI in healthcare
115 - 120 minutes
- Summarize key concepts (data -> task -> model -> evaluation -> limitation)
- Short Q&A
The healthcare mini-case:
A hospital develops a model for predicting a rare adverse event. Students receive the prevalence and confusion matrices for two models. They compare sensitivity, PPV and false positives, choose a deployment threshold, and discuss whether the model is suitable. They then learn that preprocessing occurred before the split, some patients appeared in both sets, and performance deteriorated at another hospital.
This single case covers:
- prevalence and PPV;
- model selection;
- threshold trade-offs;
- leakage;
- internal versus external validation;
- dataset shift;
- generalizability;
- clinician, developer and manager perspectives.

When?

What?


First 30 minutes of the lesson

Introduction to omics data. Discuss the different types of omics data (metabolomics, proteomics, transcriptomics etc.) and the characteristics that make omics data special (batch effects, sparse data, high dimensionality (p >> n).

Short introduction of the RNA-sequencing case study and the RNA-sequencing data processing workflow (before the count table).



60 minutes of the lesson

Students work on a case study (count table of an RNA-seq experiment):

1.        The students shortly look at the mapping statistics and try to interpret them. 
2.        The students explore the raw count table (amount of zero values, library size [=total counts per sample], number of detected genes etc.) and the metadata.
3.        The students create a PCA plot and perform hierarchical clustering on the raw count table. The students draw conclusions. 
4.        The students perform log-transformation (log2(count + 1)) and redo the PCA/clustering/drawing conclusions.
5.        The students perform variance filtering and redo the PCA/clustering/drawing conclusions. 




Last 10 minutes of the lesson

Short wrap up for the lesson (conclusions + discussion point that all different forms of omics data have their own specific challenges).

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines disinformation as an economic system: the financial incentives of the attention economy, the ad-tech machinery that pays for engagement, and the way AI has lowered the cost of producing content optimised for clicks rather than accuracy. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats disinformation not only as a content problem but as a supply chain with money at every step. The guiding question is who pays for this, and how.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from the logic of the attention economy to the plumbing of programmatic advertising to the effect of generative AI, and then to the responses. It starts with Simon's account of attention as the scarce resource and the evidence that engagement and accuracy pull apart, using the Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (2018) study of false-news spread and its documented limits. It then explains how programmatic advertising works, through real-time bidding across exchanges and demand-side and supply-side platforms, and why automated placement, indifferent to site quality, routes advertiser money to made-for-advertising and disinformation sites, at a scale the Association of National Advertisers measures in the tens of billions of dollars. It shows how generative AI has turned this into an industrial process, with thousands of AI content farms built to harvest ad revenue, and how reputable brands end up funding them without knowing. It closes on the countermeasures and their limits.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to reason about the money behind information. Students learn to follow the flow of advertising revenue from a brand's media budget to a disinformation publisher, to name the actors and mechanisms at each step, and to judge the countermeasures honestly, including why demonetisation is politically fraught and why several of its main implementers have pulled back under legal and political pressure. They then apply the EU frame: the Digital Services Act and the Code of Practice on Disinformation, now a Code of Conduct under Article 45, which carries advertising-transparency, recommender-system and demonetisation commitments. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding where a brand's or an institution's advertising may run, how to set brand-safety and inclusion rules, and how to defend those decisions when the marketplace is opaque. The teaching aim is judgement about incentives: content moderation alone does not touch the business model, and changing what gets funded is a different and harder lever.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, the attention economy: attention as the scarce resource (Simon), engagement as the currency, and why optimising for engagement diverges from accuracy; the Vosoughi et al. (2018) evidence and its limits.
15 to 40, the ad-tech machine: real-time bidding, exchanges, demand-side and supply-side platforms; made-for-advertising sites; why automated placement ignores site quality; the scale of wasted spend (ANA).
40 to 60, generative AI as an accelerant: AI content farms built for ad revenue (NewsGuard tracking since 2023); how ad money reaches disinformation publishers, and how a brand's ads end up on those sites through opaque programmatic buying rather than by choice; Google and the major exchanges are the largest single sources.
60 to 75, responses and their limits: demonetisation and follow-the-money (the Global Disinformation Index, Check My Ads, brand-safety), why it is contested, and its retreat under pressure; the EU frame (the Digital Services Act and the Code of Conduct on Disinformation).
75 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students trace the ad-revenue path for a given disinformation or AI-content-farm site, then draft a brand-safety and ad-placement policy for a named advertiser or public institution, and defend it against the transparency limits of the mark

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines the psychology of synthetic media: how AI-generated video, audio, images, and text change what audiences trust, how they judge what is real, and how public communication works when any recording can be challenged as fake. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats synthetic media as a shift in the conditions of belief, not as a detection problem to be solved with a better tool. The lecture is built around the liar's dividend: once convincing fakes are common, the mere possibility of a fake lets a speaker dismiss authentic evidence as fabricated.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from definitions to cognition to consequences to practice. It first separates deepfakes from cheapfakes and other manipulations and establishes that audiences react to the claim made about a piece of content more than to the technique behind it. It then explains the cognitive mechanisms that make synthetic content believable or persistent: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning. It then turns to the effects that matter most for a communicator. Current evidence indicates that political deepfakes are not, on average, more persuasive than other forms of misinformation, but that they destabilise trust in news and institutions and can damage the reputation of the person shown even when audiences rate the clip as not credible. The liar's dividend is presented as the sharpest form of this problem, with the experimental evidence for it and the current debate about how far it reaches video.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to work in an environment where authenticity can no longer be inferred from the medium. Students examine how repetition, reliance on social media, and motivated reasoning shape belief, why credibility ratings understate the real harm of synthetic content, and how the liar's dividend is used to avoid accountability. They then build a practical response: a verification and disclosure workflow that relies on content provenance (C2PA content credentials) and plausibility-aware checking rather than on detection alone, that meets the transparency and labelling duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act, and that communicates uncertainty without pushing audiences into indiscriminate distrust. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding under time pressure whether to publish, label, or challenge a piece of media, and explaining that decision to an audience. The teaching aim is judgement: understanding what synthetic media does to an audience, and choosing communication practices that hold up when any single piece of evidence can be called fake.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, definitions and taxonomy: deepfakes, cheapfakes, generated audio, image and text; why the claim attached to content matters more to audiences than the production method.
15 to 35, cognition: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning; the finding that higher cognitive ability and heavy social-media use change exposure, not immunity.
35 to 55, consequences: epistemic destabilisation, trust erosion, and reputational damage below the threshold of belief; the liar's dividend, the evidence for it, and the open question of how far it reaches video.
55 to 70, practice foundations: the limits of detection and warnings (the continued-influence effect and reality apathy); the elements of a provenance-first response using C2PA content credentials, plausibility-aware verification, and Article 50 labelling.
70 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students draft a verification-and-disclosure workflow for a newsroom or communications team facing a suspected deepfake, or a genuine recording that a public figure has dismissed as fake, and name the liar's-dividend risk an
